R?,ottry. ON THE THRESHOLD. A happy child, 'mid April smiles and tears, Stands on the threshold" of the opening years; A prospect fair delights her beaming eyes And makes them brighter shine with glad surprise, For life to her seems full of hope and joy, She little thinks the gold contains alloy, Nor dreams that clouds will gather o'er the sky That looks so fair to her enraptured eye; For (like young birds that feel their growing wings, And long to soar above) youth gladly springs To welcome life and its bright promisings. A few short years have quickly fled, and now, With orange blossoms on her smooth young brow A maiden, soon to take the name of wife," Stands "on the threshold" of her married life, And glances back with tender, beating heart, For from the dear loved home 'tis hard to part. Although the future promises so well De true and sweet fulfilment, who can tell? She knows in this dear nest is safe repose, And hopes that other, which her heart has chose, Will yield her life's best joys ill life shall close. *. The years again roll on, and now there stands , Upon "the threshold" of the border lands ; A matron, lovely still, though ripened age Has silvered o'er her hair, and life's last stage Is reached by slow and painful steps, that tell But a short season she on earth will dwell;, • And gazing back, she sees with eye serene, If sharp life's thorns, sweet roses bloomed between, And though her treasured gold oft dross did prove, She thanks her God, who leads her by His love Up to "the threshold" of her home above. Weleome.
Varittito. It is well to be sanguine and full of anticipation; we are the better off for our hopes even if they are never

realised. Talent is power; tact is skill. Talent makes a man respectable; tact makes him respected. Talent con- vinces: tact converts. Talent commands; tact is obeyed. Talent is something; tact is everything. Firmness and gentleness work together far more efficiently than either could alone. The strength that is allied to sweetness has a far deeper and wider influence than would be possible were it accompanied by bitter

criticism. The spirit of conciliation puts peace, love, and har- mony far above trifles; it buries petty selfishness, it inflicts no unnecessary wounds, it lends a courtesy and grace to actions, a charm to vresence, a dignity to char- acter, and a never-failing spring'of happiness to life. A great deal of discomfort arises from ever-sensitive- ness about what people may say about you or your actions. Many unhappy persons seem to imagine that they are in an amphitheatre, with the assembled world as spectators, whereas they are playing to empty benches

all the while. Dr. Donovan, despite his poverty, was a bit of a wag. "Your family," said a friend, "is Irish, and I believe, illestrious. How is it, then, that you do not follow the custom of your country, and style yourself Dr. O'Dono- van?" "Really, my good sir, lam so deeply in debt," he replied, "that I do not care to owe any more." Old Captain Starbuck, of Nantucket, a philosophical ore' leee-dog, never permitted ill-luck to damp his faith or his good ene!rite. Returning home with an empty - hold from a three years' Whaling voyage, he was boarded r by the pilot, an old acquaintande, who asked, "Waal, C•ap'n Starbuck, how many bares? Had a geed YeYage "Not 'zactly," responded the captain; "I hain'E eat. a bare of ile aboard, but I've had, a mighty'good sail !" "What keeps Mr. from kirk, James?" said a worthy minister; "I hope it is not Methodism ?" "No!" ' responded the verger, it's something worse." "What then is it. Calvinism ?" "Worse, your reverence; worse." "Surely, James, it is net Deism ?" "Much worse, an' it please your reverence, than that." "Can it be Atheism which deprives us of the best churchwarden that ever shook a box ?" "Truly," responded James, 'tis a much - more serious matter—it is rheumatism." One Reason for an Urgent Call into the country.—A French practitioner received a call one afternoon about five o'clock. from one of his country patients, a farmer who had been in town at market all day, who requested him to drive over at once to see a member of his family. The case not being urgent, the doctor replied he would ' go in the morning. 4 Oh, that will not do at all !" said the farmer. "I ask you to go now because I want a lift home, and to hire a trap will cost more than your visit." liras" Snouree TRAVEL ?—lt is a not uncommon belief with the public that when a medical man recommends a long sea voyage or foreign travel to a patient he is re- ' commending a last resource, and that he all but despairs of the case. This is not so, I assure you. No physician would advise such means to an end unless he felt quite certain that the ailing one would benefit thereby, and be I restored to health—in all probability. It is the chronic- ' ally ill who should travel—those who are suffering from some affection of an important internal organ, those who are making but poor progress in their convalescence from some acute ailment, the over-worked, the over- worried, and such as are nervous, or suffer from ennui.— aysell's Familv Magazine. - THEY KNEW THEIR Dtrree—A good story is told of a raw recruit who recently enlisted at Camp Hancock, near Atlanta. The younglellow joined the army while the country was threatening war with Mexico, and he ' intended to make a good soldier. One day he was on guard duty, and was slowly stepping along when an officer approached. After the usual salute the officer said: "Let me see your gun." The raw recruit handed over his Springfield rifle, and a pleased expression stole over his face. As the officer received the gun he said in a tone of deepest disgust: "You're a fine soldier! You've given me your gun, and now what are you going to do ?" The young Atlantian turned pale, and reaching for his hip pocket he drew a big six-shooter, easel, preparing for business, said in a voice that could not be misunderstood: "Gimme that gun, or I'll blow a hole through you in a pair 'r minutes!" The officer in- stantly decieed not to " monkey" any further with the raw recruit, and the gun was promptly surrendered. - 'This story brings to mind one that is told of a Con- • federate guard who was ones on duty over in South Cearolina. An officer was discussing war matters and remarked: "You know your duty here, do you senti- nel?" " Yes, ;sir." "Well, now, suppose they should • open on you with shells and musketry, what would you k do?" "Form a line, sir!" " What ! one man form aline, sir?" Yes, sir; form a bee line for camp, sir!" One day Beauregard, with several lesser lights, came upon •a sentinel who had taken his gun entirely to pieces and 'was greasing lock, stock, and barrel. The great General looked like a thunder cloud, but neither his flashing uniform nor the scowl on his face had any effect on the sentinel, who quietly proceeded to rub a piece of his gun. '"Say," remarked an officer, "that's Beauregard there: he's a sort of a General." "All right," said the unabashed sentinel, "If he'll wait till I get this gun together. I'll give him a sort of salute."—eitlaeta Congitution. A SCULPTOR'S HUMOUR.—James H. Beard, the artist, tells somc anecdotes of the early career of Hiram Powers, the Att en eric Sculptor, which go to show that a, „en? "n le of grim humour. When Powers went to he was engaged in making wax figures for a rcue s'• '.,um owned by a man named Dorfield. The figures r ich he mouldeS were delicate and beautiful beyond anything that was known at that time. His ingenuity in mechanics was remarkable, and Mr. Beard thinks that he would have made as great a success in mechanic arts as he did in sculpture, if he had devoted his atten- tion to the former. Therewas a popular comic singer in Powers's day at Cincinnati named Alexander Drake. Powers moulded a wax head of Drake and fashioned a I figure to match the head. One of Drake's songs, which was in great demand with audiences, was called "Love and Sausages." Powers took his wax figure to the theatre, and placed it on the stage in Drake's favourite attitude, and when the curtain rose for Drake's song, there stood before the audi- ence two Alexander Drakes, both perfectly natural. 'The people were astonished. They gazed and gazed in wonderment until the curtain went down and rose again on a single Drake. It was the wax figure, but so like e the singer that the audience cried, and shouted, and I stamped for "Love and Sausages." The figure was silent, and the curtain went down without any response ' being made to their calls. It rose again and there still Was a single Drake confronting them. This time the audience remained undemonstrative, not knowing what ,to expect. It was the true Drake. and when he pro- s cede e to sing "Love and Sausages" the mystery was intensified. For about, three days the people talked of this double Alexander Drake, and then the secret got out that it was one of Powers's freaks. At another time Powers was at work on a wax bust of Thomas Jefferson. There was a critic in Cincinnati in those days named gimnis, who had incurred the displeasure of Powers and others. lle was told one evening that the bust, was completed, and was asked to inspect it. It was in the days when the only light was from tallow candles, e • and so the room was dark he was given a candle with which tomake a close inspection of the bust. He began 'to comment upon its unnatural appearance, declaring that the colour of the flesh was not natural and so on. As he leaned down for closer inspection the burning candle was brought close to the figure, which suddenly dodged back, winked its eye, and shouted—" Don't burn me." It was Powers himself. Simms was in a terrible rage, and when the story was told some time afterwards in a paper owned by a man named Thomas, he was going to castigate the editor. Simms always denied the story, but Powers told it with great gusto.' A favourite trick oe the artist, which he often performed in the museum and in public places, was made possible by the long cloaks which it was the custom to wear in • those days. Any one who had seen the figures in a circus which are short and squat one moment and apparently ten feet high the next will understand the nature of the joke. Powers would gather his Cloak up in his hands and make himself apparently about three feet in height, and as he • passed around the museum he would gradually become taller and taller, until at last, taking the collar of his cloak and the rim of his hat in his hands, he would shove them far above his head and make himself appear very tall. All the time he would go peering around at • the sights, while most of the people were watching him as the biggest curiosity of all. For all kinds of dOIDOItIe sewing. SOME Cantons CLOClES.—England has her share of curiosities in horology, Horace Walpole had one at Strawberry Hill, given by Henry VIII. to Ann Boleyn in, 1532, which Was subsequently bought by Queen Victoria, and is now at Windsor Castle. On the weights are the initials of Henry and his second wife, united by a true lover's knot, on one, the royal motto on the other, and the words, "The most happy." Lord Leicester placed a striking clock in Cresar's Tower at Kenilworth. It had ' two faces—one south, one east—but from some unex- plained reason, when the Queen paid her celebrated visit, nothing could induce it to go. It was good Queeu Bess' who maintained in her service not only a clock-keeper, but a clockmaker, and possessed at Whitehall a wonder- ful clock, with an Ethiopian riding a rhinoceros,l accompanied by four attendants, who made obeisance when the hours struck. This recalls a curious story in cleat-lore. In 1698 one Burdeau made a clock, where Louis XIV. was seen seated on a throne, surrounded by foreign princes, all of shom did him 'homage. The inventor was persuaded in an evil hour to make a public exhibition of his work; but, unfortunately, when the effigy of William IIL made his obeisance, some of the ' machinery gave way, and threw the French king pros- trate at the feet of the English one. This, being noised abroad, reached the ears of Louis XIV. who had the un- lucky clockmaker thrown into the fastille. At Berne there is a party of wooden bears dressed in uniform of old days, who, when the hours strike, march out of &little tower, nod their heads, and return, and this same clock has pantaloon, clown, an Indian juggler, and a cock to I add to its capabilities for amusing. There is no conceit too quaint and curious, it would seem, for a clock. Some- times it is a griffin bearing an escutcheon with the dial, and rolling its eyes and opening its mouth when the 1 hours strike; sometimes it is a turret, and sometimes a ' crucifix, in which the works are concealed. Electric clocks are among the most noted modern improvements in the way of horology. They were introduced to the Royal Society in 1841 by Professor Wheatstone. One of these can communicate the time to a number of skeleton dials far away. Shepherd's electric clock in the 1851 Exhibition excited, perhaps, more interest than anything else shown at the world's fair.—From Cassell's Family Magazine for April. kW:MISTERS—whose professimal labours necessitate long in- tervals between meals—nothing will be found so exhilarating, coguorrv,n c guaranteed bw t tl ug , capablegu n toef u.ritai n 4 y pure. e xhau Bewares t e dnat o ro ss of inCtntlona.—Advt. •

"There's no use talking, I'm going to get married," said a bachelor acquaintance the other day, while busily engaged in sewing. "Hero I have worked just twenty minutes by the watch trying to get this needle threaded, and then, just as I succeeded, I pulled the thread out. Finally I got it threaded, and now, having sewed on the button good and strong, I find I have got it on the wrong side, and I have all my work to do over again. The Duke of Wellington was remarkable for the cool- ness with which he gave his directions. Even ha the heat of an engagement he wits known to give vent to a humourous observation, especially when it seemed to raise the spirits of his men. Thus, when the British were storming 13adajos, his Grace rode up whilst the balls were falling around, and, observing an artilleryman particularly active, inquired his name. He was answered "Taylor." "A very good name, too," said Wellington. "Cheer up, my men; our Taylor will soon make a pair of breeches—in the walls !" At this sally the men fm got the danger of their situation, a burst Of laughter broke from them, and the next charge carried the forts ess. div.head: AIY UNCLE'S DOG.
div.p: AIY UNCLE'S DOG.

BY CHANG LUNG. Whenever I see a lady. in the street carrying a dog in her arms, I invariably experience, a feeling of pity for her. I consider it such a sad thing that she should so lavishly waste the god-given attribute of love upon a brute beast, when there are so many worthier objects upon whom she might expend her overflowing affection; and who would appreciate it much more than a dog? Some dogs are worthy of a good deal of affection, and are anxious to repay kindness shown them. My lady's pug does not come within that category. Whenever I see him, with his dirty wet nose and watery eyes, and his pigtail an well-fed body reclining upon his owner's lap, or furs, I feel that it would do me a power of good ,to introduce my shoemaker to him. For all this, I love I dogs; but I love them for their usefulness and faithful- ness. I like to see dogs have their proper place, which iis not inside the house, but in the yard. Keep a dog in I the house and the gay and festive flea will be right there lall the time, unless his ablutions are performed oftener . than is convenient for either him or his owner. A good many people who keep a large dog pride them- selves upon the style in which their dog can chew up I other people's dogs. I have often noticed their innocent 1 and unadulterated mirth when Towser has sent off some I other dog, about half of Towser's fighting weight, giving expression to his sentiments like an ungreased cart- wheel. There seems to be about the same difference in dogs that there is in people; some are bullies, and some are the reverse. I had an uncle, now dead, who kept a yard dog which he called Rock. Rock was a very ornery dog to look at, but he was generally at home if any stranger dog called and gave him sass. He was the kind of mixture of dog that anyone could hazard a guess about as to his breed without any fear of being contradicted. He was of the middle-height and weight, and was in fair condition. By using Mrs. Allen's hair restorer he had got a coat on him that almost defied any attempt of his foes to get a mouthful of dog. Hewes copper-plated throughout, and had a set of cast-steel teeth of his own manufacture; and which he kept in excellent working condition by occasionally pulverising broken pots and old cans during his moments of leisure. He never found out that he could fight, consequently he didn't carry his head out of plumb, or walk about with his thumbs in his waistcoat armholes. In fact, be was such a low-bred dog that he was willing to romp and play tig with anybody's dog, and was therefore beloved or respected by both friends and foes. I remember being out for a walk one Sunday after- noon with my uncle and Rock, when we came across one of the small detachments of the great army of pigeon . marchers and dog fighters which are to be met with any Aim Sunday afternoon about the canal banks and fields. They had with them a fine bulldog, which we found out afterwards was being trained for a big prize fight. Some of the party, as soon as they saw Rock going near the other dog, began to try to incite their animal to try a mouthful of him. Their dog expressed his willingness to oblige by a preliminary snarl. One of the more sar- castic of the squad said to my uncle, "You had better call your dog away, or he'll . get eaten." My uncle said. "Well, he never has been eaten, and I don't think he will be now if you'll let the dogs alone." By this time the other dog. with constant incitements, given in whispers, had got hold of a mouthful of hair on Rock's neck, and Was maintaining his hold vary zealously. Not being a very fly dog Rock looked at my uncle for instructions, and he, addressing the men, said, "I think you had better .call that dog of yours off." One of them' very likely the owner, said "Yo mun co id off yorsel." My uncle sim- ply remarked "Go on, Rock; shake him !" When my uncle made the remark the squad was sitting peacefully on the canal bank, but when Rock commenced operationp there was an immediate redistribution of seats. Rock had that bulldog in seven different positions at once: he threw him over his head; he mopped the floor with him; he smacked him against the wall, and then he ran him against a pigeon marcher who had a basket, and knocked him down. There would have been no distinguishing that there were two dogs if they had been both of a colour; as it was, there was nothing definite to be seen but flashes of white as Rock put the foe through his evolutions. After Rock had per- formed on him for about five minutes, he rolled him down the bank into the canal, when it was seen that the animal was too helpless to crawl out, and his owner had to rush in to save him. My uncle asked them if they had any more dogs that wanted eating. They didn t reply, for a great peace had settled upon them. Rock's lire and burglar-proof hide was found to be intact, and he was ready to, play tig. with any dog that might be siren* his way. At my uncle's house there was a large yard, about fifteen feet inside the gateway of which was Rock's domicile. When Rock was at home he generally wore an eighteen carrot steel albert to his watch, which some- what impeded his motions 'when any of his foes paid him a hurried visit. As he could not take off his watch- guard without a little assistance some of his foes had a high old time of it. This used to delight the owners of them, and especially one who used to pass every day about tea time. This cuss was a swell who was learning , the cotton business at a mill close by. He made a point of inviting his dog—a large black retriever— Le :have a taste of Rock every time he passed, and this occurred so often, and so regularly, that my aunt got to noticing the daily scuffle about the same hour. One day she stood in the passage of the side door, facing Rock's kennel, and heard this embryo calico manufac- trner setting his dog on to Rock, and saw the brief, uneven fight that ensued, though she was invisible to the owner of the retriever. She kept quiet until the two had gone away, and then she said—" Never mind, Rock, lad; you shall have a chance to-morrow." Rock looked his thanks, wagged his stump of a tail, and lay down, to wait patiently for the coming of that morrow whery he should prove the truth of the old axiom, that every dog has his day. ef,... f.,15 The morrow came, so did the dog and the man. About a quarter of an hour before the advent of the man and hie dog my aunt took Rock's albert off, and made him go into his kennel and stop there, while she herself stood in the passage, just out of sight, and waited patiently- with a heavenly snigger on her nose that be- tokened' fun. She had made one preparation for the con- flict which I had not noticed, and that was the placing of a dripping-wet long mop just outside the door. Pre- sently, the welcome footstep could be heard jauntily coming down the street, and, as if to give notice that they were on the warpath, his dog gave vent to a bark of challenge. It was an affecting sight to see my aunt when she heard that challenge. The celestial smile on her nose deepened; her shoulders humped themselves up, and she clenched her hands with a gentle clench like the hug of a bear. As the newspaper e say, "In less time than' it takes to tell it," the- musical voice of the budding cotton lord was heard giving gentle words of encouragement to Carlo to shake him. But Rock shot out of his kennel as it he had a good deal to do before the day was ended. The air was rat once filled with most dreadful and' direful yells, that almost' made one's spine curl upwards. It was something like what a. cartload of various-sized cans would sound if tumbled down a flight of stone steps altogether. As Rock made' a dash for the foe, my aunt made a dash for the. mop, seized it and landed the owner of the foe a full broadside in !the face 'with it, and'would have repeated the dose, but!was de- feated in the attempt by his having a sudden desire to leave the seene.of action, which he put into practice at once, shouting as he ran, "Here, Carlo; here, Carlo." Carlo wanted to gob. but he discovered that he had a ivery pressing engagement on which he couldn't neglect. ,His appearance when my aunt called Rock off him was picturesque; he looked like-an overgrown mop that wis casting its coat. He carried one of his forelegs as if it had been badly fixed' on with a tack and had worked 'loose, and he seemed' as if he wanted to carry the other 'three but hadn't time. li,br a long time after that it was 'a treat to watch Carlo pass that gate, which he did at full speed on the opposite side of the street,. with his tail out of sight,. and with a yelp just as he caught sight of Rock. . I bought a doe out of a litter the other day_ I don't know why r bought him,, unless it was because—as the owner told me—he was a first-rate bred dog. His style of architecture was the isiewfounaland, of a mammoth breed, and he was six or eight months old. -- I' gave a half-crown for-him, and I rued at my bargain as soon as I had paid for him, because I bethought me that I had no use for a dog and didn't want one at all. I went and bought a chain for a shilling to lead him home with. The previous owner fastened the chain round his neck and gave me the other end, and told me I was all right. I didn't think I was all right, and I didn't feel:as right as 13 might have felt. I started to go, but the dog didn't seem inclined that way. He sat down on the thick end of his tail, and planted his forefeet firmly on the floor, like they fix planks when they prop a house up with them. I stroked and. patted him and put on my most persuasive manner and smile to induce him to come along, but he con- tinued to doubt my intentions. He seemed reluctant to forsake the friends of his youth. I took a firm grip of my end of the ehain and started off as if 7 meant busi- ness; he followed, but he followed the way a pot dog would have, followed; he slid on his foundation and forefeet. I didn't know how to make him walk, but the friend I bought him from did. He gave him what he called a lifter, and then we went gaily slang for a hun- dred yards or so. / had to go, for he seemed to have got it into his head that I had obliged him with the lifter, and he -did his best to avoid being lifted again. As he was going at a rate that was not conducive either to my comfort or dignity. I thought I would put a slight check upon his impetuosity. ' SO I gave a gentle two-horse power jerk at the chain and yanked him over on his back on the dirty pavement. This filled him with ardour and animation. After rolling completely over in the dirt, he jumped to his feet and made one noble dash for liberty, but finding that liberty did not lie in that direction, he changed his tactics and tried to surround me. He succeeded completely. He sur- rounded me twice before I had time to argue OA matter with him. When he had done with we he had managed to get rid of the dirt that he had picked up off the pave- ment. I had it. lie had painted on my trousers a picture of a siorm at sea. After I had got out of the tangle I felt that I wanted to go home. People had begun to stop. They appeared to be anxious to help me. I didn't want any help. I was warm, very warm; and I felt, that there was no place like home. The dog had re- sumed his sitting posture. He evidently had deter-

div.p: A MODERN MIRACLE. THE MOST MARVELLOUS EXPERIENCE OF ONE OF
GLOUCESTER'S CITIZENS. (Gloucester Journal, April 30.)

The readers of this paper were more or less amazed at a most remarkable statement from one of our citizens, which appeared in this paper on the 16th inst. So unusual were the circumstances connected with it, and so much comment did it occasicn on the street and in social circles, that a representative of this paper was commissioned to investi- gate its details and verify its facts. The article referred to was a statement made by Mr. J. H. Kilminster, of King's Home, Gloucester, that after having lain at the point of death for some weeks, given up by both physicians and friends, be had completely and wonderfully regained his usual health. Mr. Kilminster was found by our reporter, and upon being questioned, said : " Yes, air, the statement is true, every word of it. For . nearly a year I suffered from acute kidney disease, which finally became complicated with dropsy and severe asthmatic attack,. My condition was most deplorable. I had the beat medical advice that was to be obtained, who consulted With my regular medical adviser, a well-known and skilful man. They informed me that my water was full of albu- men and tube casts, and gave me little hope that I should ever recover. All these months I could net lie down on ac- count of the asthma and dropsy, and could not rise from my chair without assistance. On October 23rd last I had an unusually severe attack, which came near ending my life. Mr friends concluded I must die, and hurriedly brought in My family physician. As all the regular methods had failed, be saw no objection to my using Warner's SAFI Care, of which he had heard good reports, though never having had any experience in its use himself. A bottle was obtained for me, and I received almost instant relief. At this time nay breathing was so bad that it could be heard across the street; I was bloated from head to foot, and my water wee thick with albumen. My physician watched the progresa of ts 9 case carefully under the use of Warner's SAFE Cure, and each fortnight, when the water was tested, he found the albumen gradually growing less, until it was entirely free, and I Flood recovered my usual health." " Your experience has certainly been moot wonder- ful." " Yes; and my recovery so remarkable that it has excited Much attention, and physicians as well as others have in- vestigated it thoroughly ; and I am glad, for I feel that the reaulta of such a wonderful cure should be known to the thousands in all parts of the land who are suffering from troubles of the kidneys, liver, or heart, in some if their Many dangerous forms." Our reporter thanked Mr. Kilminster for his very frank and clear statement, and was about leaving the house, When a gentleman stepped up to him and inquired If he Were seeking information about Mr. Kilminater's illness and recovery. The scribe replied that he was, whereupon the gentleman said— " Ss am I, and I have come all the way from London for that very purpose. Kidney troubles seem to be alarmingly increasing all over the country, and I have a very near re- lative who is afflicted much as Mr. Kilminster was. I have been to see several of Mr. Kilminster's friends ; and I tell You, sir, it is simply wonderful." " What did they say I" asked the man of news. "Why, sir, they fully confirmed everything Mr. Kilmin- ster has said. Mr. J. Ward, Bohannom House, Wootton, Who was a candidate for Parliament at the last election,and is now a member of the School Board, Town Council, and one of the Board of Guardians, stated that he has known Kilminster all his life as a staunch friend and sup- Porter. He took great interest in his case, and watched With sorrow, from day to day, the gradual approach of death. He shook hands with him for the last time, as be Was convinced that he could not live, his death being ex- pected every hour. He afterwards learned that he was improving, and on calling upon him found this to be the case, and that a mtdicine called Warner's SAFE Cure was doing wonders for him. He said that it had performed a miracle for him almost beyond belief, and that it was a most wonderful case. Mr. J. Williams, Sorth g te • str t , said that " Mr. Kil- Minster'a recovery was a surprise to every one that knew him. We never expected to see him out of his house again, but expected to go to his funeral. His recovery is singu- larly unaccountable, and speaks wonders for the Warner's Salm Cure." Mr. Franklin; Gloucester, electioneering agent, said :—" I have known Mr.Kilminster all his life, and consider his case little less than a miracle. L visited him constantly while be was ill, and understood from his physidian that he could never recover. Ho was the colour of ashes when I saw him, very much bloated from head to font, and was scarcely able to breathe, and there seemed no possibility of his living. At this stage he commenced taking Warner's SAFE Cure, and rapidly recovered. It is certainly a most wonderful Medicine." 'Mr. G. W. Holden, chemist, 75. Northgate-street, said : " Yes, I both know, and have heard of Mr. Kilminster's serious illness and his recovery. He purchased most of the Warner's SAVE Cure from me. The case is a very wonder- ful one, and speaks velumes for the medicine. We are sell- ing large quantities, and, from the reports of it, have every confidence that it is a specific for all kidney and liver diseases." The conclusions from the statements above made, which come to the newspaper man as well as the general public, !mist be two-fold. First: That a modern miracle of heal- lag has been performed in our midst, and that too by the aim- Pleat means, and one which is within the reach of everyone; and, secondly: That testimonials of such high character and so outspoken in tone conclusively prove the value of the remedy, and its superior nature to the proprietary articles with which the public have been flooded. "The greater includes the less," and the remedy which has been proven valuable,so wn to death's a doer, eh:es, moat td unquestionably life after it was brought all miner troubles, which a neetiebl y unless certain taken in re so time.disastrousonb e The remedy which cared Mr. K ilm in ter, and of which the above gentlemen speak, can be procurede of all chemists and medicine vendors in the United Kingdom, at 45 65 per bottle, or direct of the manufacturers, H. H. WARNER & CO., 47, Farringdon Street, Landon, E.C.

Seventy-five panes of glass in the Protestant Church, St Ifilkee, are reported to have been maliciously broken 0/1 Saturday. It is stated that so- Dublin magistrates have become disqualified for sitting at licensing sessions, owing to their having taken shares in Guinness's brewery. The Freeman's Journal says it is rutnoured that the Government intend the prosecution of another priest Prominently connected with the Nationalist cause in the s of Ireland. Mr. Parnell has approved of applying immediately for the Speaker's warrant to issue is writ, to elect a member t'lf Parliament for North-East Cork, in the room of Mr. ▪ a,. my, resigned ; and that Mr. William O'Brien, editor I,''' United Ireland, who is on his way to Canada, should elected to the vacancy, despite his objection to enter rarliament. Seventy militiamen on their way to the Curragh, for .1. -raining, arrived at Kildare on Monday. They created a,riot, overturning carts and doing other damage; and Shopkeepers closed their premises. Half a doten police- ,'''en who attempted to quell the disturbance were —▪ t-agely beaten Nineteen arrests were made. . The House met at 4 15 p.m. EAYLINGDEN Twatwirs.—The Haslingden and Oswald- twistle Tramways Bill was read a second time.

div.head: NEW HEBRIDES.
div.p: THE NEW HEBRIDES.

The EARL of HARROWBY, who called attention to the condition of affairs in the New Hebrides and asked what course was intended to be taken with reference to the subject by Her Majesty's Government, complained of the continued presence of French soldiers in the islands. and said private correspondence he had received showed that the French were throwing up fortifications and making preparations for a permanent stay there. Lord SALISBURY, in reply, said that both France and England had engaged not to annex the New Hebrides, and-there was no doubt that at that moment the French Government was in occupation:of those islands. They had, however, assured her Majesty's Government that they had no intention to permanently occupy the New Hebrides, and that no definitive character ought to be attached to their action. They informed her Majesty's Government that they had been induced to take the steps they had taken solely in consequence of the out- rages that had occurred. He believed that the French Ambassador Was likely to make a communication of some importance on the subject during the present week.

---- MISCELLANEOUS.—Lord SODELRY alluded to the present Aystene of retirement in the navy; and Lord Etruni- Bronx, in reply, stated that to remove the block which at present existed. in the promotion of naval lieutenants, it was proposed by the Government to increase the num- ber of commanders by 270.—Replying to tho Earl of I Belrnore, Earl CADOGAN stated that there was no objec- tion to a return of the loans made to owners of land in Ireland by the Board of Public Works in Ireland for the improvement of their estates. The House adjourned at 7 15 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MON-DAY,

The Speaki.,ook the chair at 4 p.m. IMPRISONED F3OCIALISTB.—The HOME SECRETARY, reply- ing to Mr. Pickersgill, said that he saw no reason to interfere in the matter of the six months' imprisonment passed by Mr. Do Rutzen upon seven Socialists at the Varylebone Police Court last week.

THE CRIMES BILL.—THE CLOSURE APPLIED. The House resumed the consideration in Committee of the Criminal Law Amendment (Ireland) Bill. On the first clause, which gives power to hold preliminary in- quiries in proclaimed districts, Mr. T. HEALY moved the first amendment, leaving out the general words " pro- claimed districts," in order to insert certain specified counties with a view of securing the application of the inquiry clause to Belfast Mr. A. J. BALFOUR declined to give any assurances ex- cept that the Act would be administered impartially. Mr. GLADSTONE, enlarging on the disorder prevalent in the Protestant counties, emphasised the necessity of applying the bill to those counties, but suggested the withdrawal of the amendment and the discussion of the question at a later stage. Lord R. Cauttcrutz agreed that this would be the more convenient course, but in answer to the allegation as to the condition of the North, ridiculed the notion of com- parirfg the Belfast rioters with the Kerry moonlighters. After some further discussion with reference to mis- carriages of justice in Belfast, the amendment was-with- drawn. / Mr. M. HEALY moved an amendment to the same clause, to limit the right of the Attorney-General for Ireland to order a preliminary inquiry to thoSe cases where, owing to intimidation or other improper cause, evidence has been withheld. The ATTORNEY-GENERAL for ENGLAYD said the Govern- mcnt could not accept the amendment.—SisC. RUSSEL suggested that the words in the amendment "has been withheld" should be altered into "is not forthcoming."

Mr. W. REDMOND supported the amendment. The hon. member was twice called to order, being first told by the Chairman that he was "discoursing at large," and, on the second occasion, that "he did not appear to have apprehended the subject matter of the amend- ment."—The amendment was further supported by Mr. T. Roberts, Mr. P. J. Pow,r, Mr. Clancy, Mr. E. Har- rington, Mr. Cox, Mr. Murphy, Mr. M. J. Kenny, Mr. Chance, and Dr. Commins. The House divided— For the amendment llO
Against Mr. M. HEALY proposed that in putting the machinery of the clause into operation the Attorney-General should not act on his own initiative, but should obtain the sanction of the High Court.

The SOLICITOR-GENERAL thought that this was an amendment which the Government could not be reason- ably expected to accept. Mr. CHANCE supported the amendment, which was opposed by Mr. A. ELLIOTT, who could not see why the system of preliminary inquiry in force in Scotland should not be extended to Ireland. (Ministerial cheers.) Mr. GLADSTONE observed that the representation of the Scotch people in that House gave him the impression that it would be impossible to resort to a worse authority on Scotch opinion than his hon. and learned friend. (Opposition cheers.) His lion. and learned friend (Mr. Elliot) had stated that provisions similar to this were passed five years ago, and were about to be renewed three years ago. Rut he entirely overlooked the funda- mental and essential difficulty that if that provision was made five years ago it was directed exclusively against crime—(Opposition cheers)—and according to their con- tention, confirmed, as they thought, by the language of the Government, this was not a bill dealing exclusively with orime—(Ministerial cries of " Oh")—but dealing with acts which were for the first time going to be made crimes. (Opposition cheers.)

THE CLOSURE. Mr. W. REDMOND having spoken, and charactesised the bill as infamous, Mr. W. H. SMITH rose and moved, "That the question be now put." (Ministerial cheers, and shouts of "1o" and" Shame" from the Nationalists.) The House divided, when there were— For the motion 257 Against

The result was hailed with loud Ministerial cheers. Colonel NOLAN, seated and with his hat on, in accord- ance with practice when a division is proceeding, raised a point of order in connection with the division. (Loud cries of "Order" from the Conservatives.) He wished to know whether it was in order for a number of mem- bers to stand at the glass door and hoot members going into the" No" division lobby. (Ministerial laughter and Home Rule cheers.) The CHAIRMAN: Of course, such conduct is disorderly. (Cheers.) Mr. M. Healy's amendment, as amended, was then put, the Chairman declaring that the " Noes" had it . .
On a division there vcted— For the amendment 142
Against

An ainei;drnent to exempt the application of the clause when any person has been made amenable for the offence proposed to be inquired into, also moved by Mr, M. Healy, was discussed for three-quarters of an hour and then withdrawn, after which the Committee ad- journed. The House adjourned at 2 a.m. HOUSE OF LORDS.--Tcesney.
The Lord Chancellor took his ;eat at-471-6-17).m. CuErroms.--The Customs Consolidation Act (1876) Amendment Bill was lead a second time.

GOVERNMENT OF MALTA.—Replying to Earl de la Warr, the Earl of ONSLOW said the Council of the Governor of Malta had been dissolved, and as a period of three months must elapse before the election of the new Coun- cil, it had been thought desirable to take steps as soon as possible to enable the constituencies to express their opinion upon the new scheme of constitutional changes. He hoped to produce papers in the course of a day or two.

- AN EXPLANATION.—The Marquis Of SALISBURY, with reference to a reply he gave on Monday evening, said it appeared that there was one of her Majesty's ships stationed at the New Hebrides, and always had been. Their Lordships rose at 4 35 pm. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUF-SDAY.

The Speaker took the Chair at 4 p.m. In reply to Mr. Dillon, Sir JAS. FERGUSSON said the House would be infor • eid se to the nature and results of the negotiations now going en between Sir H. D. Wolff and the Porte on the subject of the British occupation of Egypt as soon RS the public interest permitted. In reply to Mr. James Rowlands, the CIIANCELLOR of the Excuranan said the mint were now issuing bronze coins in order to meet the de rand caused by the with- drawal of the French bronze coins from circulation. About £6,000 of French bronze coins had been received from the ;public, and it was estimated that the total amount that would be received would not exceed £12,000. "THE TIMES" AND THE IRISH MEMBERS.

_ Sir C. LEWIS rose to call attention to a serious breach of the privileges of the House, a member being charged with wilful and deliberate falsehood in the House by The Times of Monday. Tie referred at length to the article on rarneilism and Crime, in which The Times charged Mr. Dillon with knc,wingly reakio.g statements at varianoe with the fact in regard -to Mr. P. J. He maintained that the House was the-guardian of its own honour and never before hadrsucheiarges been made against one of its members and owed to pass un- notieecL-The extracts from the article havine, been read by the Clerk at the table Sir C. firms moved that the words constituted a breach of the privileges of the House.

Mr. J. Drizorr said he had not the slightest objection , 0 urge against the motion, except the want of time. (Hear, hear.) He asked the Speaker at what stage it would be more convenient to make a detailed reply to the attack upon himself. If the House decided that the article was a breach of privilege, he would be quite ready to make his statement, but required a little time* for preparation. The SPEAKER said if the House decided the motion int the affirmative, that motion could be followed by another requiring the printer and publisher to attend at the bar. Tithe debate was adjourned, it would take prezedence of other business on a later day. Mr. W. H. AN INCORRIGIBLE.— At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, Mary Waldron, a Widow, was summor.ed for neglecting to sod her son to school. The school attend- ance officer Mr. Pegg) stated that the defendant's son had net been near the school for seven weeks.—The defendant said she could not manage her son, and she was quite powerless over him. She asked the Bench to commit him to some Industrial School. A letter was read from a Catholic priest at Gelborne stating that the lad in question was most incorrigible, and, "in a word," the letter con- tinued, "he is too clever a rascal to ream abroad, and for his own aid others' sakes, he should be sent to a reforma- tory."—The Bench made an order for the committal of the boy to St. Anne's Industrial School at Liverpool. DISORDERLY CONDUCT AT GOLBORNE.—At the Newton Petty Seesions, on saturdar, James Handley and Thomas Grundy were summoned for being drunk and disorderly in High-street, Golborne, on the 23rd ult., and they were each fined 5s and costs.—Defendant Handley was also summoned for assaulting the other defendant, Grundy. He was bound over to keep the peace for eix months.—Thomas Handley, trother of the last-named defendant, was afterwards fined 5s and costs for drunkenness.—John Waldron and Andrew Noon were charged with committing a breach of the peace he fighting together on the 23rd ult., at Gelborne, and Frank Charles, Michael McGrail, James Noon, and Thomas Gilli- gan, were charged with being disorderly. It was stated by Police-constables Ratcliffe and Lewis that the two first. named defendants fought in a field near Tanner's-lane, Gl- borne, and the other defendants were disorderly. The ma- gistrates dismissed the summonses against Charles James Noon and Gil lighan and ordered other defendants to be bound over to keep the prod.—Andrew Noon and Patrick McGrail were next charged with committing a breach of the pea eby fighting on the 23rd ult. The summons was withdr wn. McGrail was subsequently ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for six months.

COMMITTAL OF A. CLERGYMA.M.—The Rev. James Bell Cox, vicar of St. Margaret's, Prince's-road, Liverpool, wnose appeal against a judgment of Lord Penzance for Ritualism was dismissed in the House of Lords the other day, was arrested on Thursday morning under the warrant of Lord Penzance, and taken to Lancaster Castle, where he will be imprisoned for contumacy. The rev, gentleman had been awaiting the atrival of the sheriff's officer for two or three days, and was in complete readiness. After taking a hurried leave of his wife, one of his churchwardens, and a few of his parishioners, he was driven in a cab to Walton Gaol.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON. THURSDAY.

IThe course of the Coercion Bill thiougli—c-o-m—m-it- I tee, cumbering at its best, was, on Tuesday night, interrupted by a startling incident. For weeks the "Times" has been trailing its coat tail before the Irish members and imploring someone to tread upon it. Its reductor of stale charges against Mr. Parnell and his friends fell decidedly flat. Day after day it discussed ;hem in its leading columns, but nobody else would. The shrieking demand to be prosecuted met with silence equally contemptu- ous and embarassing. At a moment when the whole thing was being smothered in its own smoke, Sir Charles Lewis appears upon the scene, and the whole aspect of affairs is suddenly changed. Very little has been heard of the former member for Derry since heiwas nada a baronet. Why this honour should have been conferred upon him is one of the things the House cannot understand. He has never done any Service to his party. On the contrary, he has, from his earliest appearance in political life, been a cause of embarassment to them. He reappears in the rOle he has already made famous. It was in NM that he interrupted the business of Parliament by a ridiculous motion calling theprinters of the "Times" and the "Daily News" to the Bar of the House, because those journals had printed, among evidence publicly given in the Committee Room, a letter written by Mt. Lowe. Mr. Disraeli, then leader of the House, never forgave the member for Derry for dragging him into a false position. In a moment of weak- ness the Government supported • the motion, and when the printers appeared at the Bar, Mr. Dis- raeli himself moved that they be dismissed. It was at this epoch that Mr. Lewis's white waistcoat be- came familiar to the public through the agency of the "World," then just coming. into prominence. Mr. Healy was mistaken in saying that Mr. Lewis made a complaint to the House about the liberty taken with his white waistcoat. What he did was criminally to prosecute the publisher of the "World," the case being dismissed having brought permanent advantage to the young paper. In 1875 Mr. Charles Lewis made himself very un- popular with his leaders and his party by his incon- venient interposition. But he was then quite an idol of the Carlton compared with the position he holds to-day. It is but justice to the Government to say that to no one more than to them was the new baronet's action of Tuesday night a surprise. 'But as any child, having a box of matches may set fire to a house, so may any fussy, vain, stubborn, indiscreet man having a seat in the House of Com- mons, drag his party throught the mud. Sir Charles Lewis's motion being before the House, the Govern- ment were obliged to take note of it, and if Mr.' Smith blundered throughout in the most egregious manner, there is nothing in his previous career as 'leader of the House that would justify expectation of other result. Wholly unprepared to deal with an unexpected difficulty, he nervously moved the ad- journment of the debate, with the result that the whole of Tuesday night was wasted, in discussing that suggestion. Having taken council on Wednes- day morning, ministers came down at noon and made the astounding proposal that Mr. Dillon should prosecute the "Times" at large with the National Exchequer at his disposal and the Attorney-, General to lead his case! It is impossible to con- ceive the frame of mind in which a dozen business men more or less of average merit could read such a conclusion. It was, of course, contemptuously rejected by the Irish members, and now Mr. Glad- stone 'has formally undertaken to press on the House the acceptance of a Select Committee before which the charges of the " Times " can be thoroughly and dispassionately sifted. In the mean- time public business is stopped, and in Conservative circles Sir Charles Lewis is boycotted. Lady Resebery, like Lady Hayter, does a conspic- uous service to the Liberal party by, from time to time, entertaining it. It sometimes, however, happens that social attractions clash with business engagements, and the latter 'suffer. Thus it was on ' Monday night when Lady Rosebery was "At' Home" at Lansdowne House. This was her first party after returning from India, and irwould be difficult to imagine anything done on a more princely scale. Seventeen hundred invitations were issued, and I should say that at one time or another betwee&half-past ten and twelve sixteen hundred put in an appearance. Invitations were showered among members on the Liberal side, and were ac- cepted with an alacrity that played havoc with divisions in Committee on the Coercion Bill. Mem- bers came and went, but it was easy at any hour of the evening to count a quorum spread over the splendid suite of rooms. The result was that the Conservative majority in the House of Commons ran up considerably, the Closure being carried by 122, the biggest majority yet obtained. A good many members left in time to put in a late appear- ance, or the state of affairs would have been more disastrous still. But it required an effort to tear one's self away from the fascinating scene. Per- haps politics predominated as represented by the company, but amid the throng were rrognisable most of the leaders in art, science, and literature. It is with unfeigned pleasure I record an action of the present Government, wherein they show to ad- vantage as compared with their predecessors. When Primrose Day came round under the rule of a Liberal Home Secretary, the *sore of. the rotting primrose wreaths round the hapless statue of Lord Beaconsfield in Parliament-square reniained far into the spring. Probably the reason for this was due to an ill-conceived feeling of generosity. To have swept away the rubbish after it had served its purpose would probably have been taken in Prim- rose Habitations as an act of political jealousy. Mr. Matthews, free'at least from the possibility of such a charge, has had the flowers already removed, in- cluding the advertisement from the gentleman in Hong Song which appears every year, and which is perhaps the cheapest among the annuals. By the way, 'J heard the other day from an authoritative source the origin of the craze which associates the name of Lord Beaconsfield with the primrose. As a matter of fact, he never expressed bY word or deed a preference for the flower. Lord Rowton once told me that if Mr. Disraeli cared for any particular flower it was the violet. But the thing he cared most for in nature was the peacock's tail that used to spread itself out before him as he lounged on the lawn at Hughenden. It will be remembered that what started the fable was the appearance at the funeral of a wreath of primroses, sent by the Queen, inscribed "His favourite flower." This was natur- ally taken as meaning Lord Beaconsfield's favourite flower. But, as a matter of fact, the Queen was alluding to a preferenceof the Prince Consort's, and to her mind the personal pronoun was sufficient to indicate the individual who always filled her thoughts. The London Press has something to learn from its country cousins in the matter of main- taining its dignity when attempts are made to snub it. From time to time one reads with pleasure how the Press of a particular town or district, taking common action, resent an attempt made,by bump- tious officialism to treat it without proper con- sideration-. It will hardly be believed that with respect to one important function of the year the potent London Press, with two exceptions, permits itself to be despitefully treated. Years ago, when the institution of the Royal Academy Dinner was started, the "Times' was the eclipse of London journalism, the rest being nowhere. Accordingly a ticket for the dinner was sent to the" Times," which had the exclusive report of the proceedings. In this, 'as in other respects, the Royal Academy has learned nothing. It does not seem to know that there are in London daily newspapers with three or four times the circulation of the "Times." But the old custom is retained, and the "Times" only is in- vited to the banquet, though of late years a stipula- tion has been made that it shall supply a proof of

its report to the " Observor" and to the London dailies. Since the "Daily News" came under new editorship it.has declined to be a party to such an insulting arrangement. The "Standard," under Mr. Mudford's direction, has taken the same line, and on Monday both these papers came out without the slightest reference to the Academy Dinner, a report of which filled five columns of the "Times." The other morning papers meekly took their proof, and gave more or less full reports. If all, on a single occasion, followed the lead of the "Standard" and tbe "Daily News," their contemptuous treatment by the Academy would not be repeated in the fel.. lowing year. There are dinners and dinners at the Mansion House, varying as the stars in magnltude. There are the ordinary duty dinners, at which Aldermen, Town Councillors, and city friends are liberally gorged. There are regulation dinners to Her Majesty's judges, to Her Majesty's Ministers, and to other honoured guests, which are great improve- ments on the Aldermanic feeds. But by common consent the dinnei given last night by the Lord Mayor to the Colonial Delegates was the most bril- liant the Mansion House has seen for some years. There were some half dozen citizens in scarlet gowns, who have Passed the chair'. But for the rest the Lord Mayor had secured the attendance of the best society in London. It was one of the rare occp.sions when ladies were invited, a circum- stance which of itself lent grace and charm to the occasion. It was a fitting climax to the hospitality which London has offered to our Colonial cousins, and agreeably followed the cold luncheon eaten in a back room at Windsor Castle earlier in the day, when the chair of the hestess was conspicuously empty. This week will practically see a conclusion of the Conference, which, I hear, has been produc- tive of substantial results. One meets the Colonial Delegates everywhere just now, and in conversation with them finds strong unanimity of satisfaction at. their reception in London both in social and busi- ness aspects.

A Paris correspondent, in a lengthy telegram cc* attention to a fact concerning which he says the inatists in Paris appear more anxious than about thei Pagny affair. Hardly a singlei vessel has been left in the North and West, and 016 opinion prevails that this extraordinary display of navati force has a special object. The supposition is th France meditates a coup in Egypt, or that in case of war on the frontier, Italy, as the ally of Gerynany,woul be the scene of vigorous action by France in the bom-1 bardment of the coast towns. The Timrs correspondent at Mandalay, tel-graphind uuder date May Ist, says t—During the past week several skirmishes with Dacoits are reported. In every instance the result was successful, and our casualties were very trifling. The 4th and 6th Brigades have amalgamated under Brigadier Lowe, C. 8., a detachments of his force have had a series successful engagements with Dacoits and insurgen The health of General Lowe's troops continues to excellent. The Irrawaddy is rising rapidly. Mandala is stfll very peamful. Captain A. W. Randle, 10 Madras infantry, was killed on the 30th April, in a skir-I mish with dacoits, near Sidoka. No details have yet boem received.

NEN? YORK. THURSDAY.—A general strike has come menced in the Connellsville (Pennsylvania) coke region, 13,000 men being idle. It is not expected that trouLte will arise unless fresh bands should be imported to take the place of the men on strike. EARTHQUAKE. SHOCKS IN CENTRAL AMERICA. NEW YORK, WEDNESDAY,—Later details respecting the earthquake yesterday state the shecks extended s•mth-weat as far as the Pacific Coast. A minute after the first quiver the highest cliff of Chivato mountain fell, causing clouds of ' dust to arise, which aTpeared in the distance as if a vol. canic eruntion bad occurred. No casualities are reported. NEW YORK, THURSDAY, 6 AM.—Later reports from the South-Western btates annomme that earthquake shocks con- tinue. The seismic disturbance has been general through. out Southern Arizona. At Benson six distinct shocks have been felt since yesterday morning. It is stated that ai undoubted volcanic crater has been formed on a mountain 20 miles distant from the town, and is in active eruption. TERRIBLE COLLIERY EXPLOSION IN BRITISH
COLUMBIA. GREAT LOSS OF LIFE.

Vtcrortra. WinnEsrimr.—A terrible explosion of firedamp has occurred in a coal mine at Manaimo, Vancouver Island. Altogether 150 miners are entombed in the workings, and their rescue is considered hopeless, the mine being on fire.

Twelve of the miners entombed in the coal mine at Man. aim.., Vancouver Island, Suave been recovered. Some of these were dead when brought to the pit's mouth, and the rest are seriously burned. Little hope is entertained of rescuing alive any of those stilt remaining in the mine. The scene around the abaft is described as heartrending, vicroma, Burma COLUMBIA, THURSDAY, 1 A.M.—The fire in the Nanaimo mine is still burning. Of the 133 miners still entombed 75 are Chinagnmen.

[CENTItiL NEWS TEM:GRA:Ai NEW Yons, TarrnsnaY MORSTING.—The latest details concerning the terrible colliery explosion in British Colume bia state that the mine belongs to the Victoria Coal Corn. patty. Of the 150 miners who were entombed 12 have been rescued, although most of them are fearfully injured. There is unhappily every reason to fear that:the other poor fellows hay( been burnt alive in the mine.

LORD HARTINGTON AT LEEDS. Lord ifartington was the pancipal speaker at a Unionist demonstration held ha the Coliseum at Leeds on Wednesday night. He said he regretted to find himself in acute and strong difference with the Liberal patty ; but his position seemed to bim inevi, table, when he considered the great question at issue—the continuance of legislative union between Great Britain anc/ Irelant The present Government was not a Tory Govern- ment. Those who composed it had sunk for the time their political principles In order that a great national ob- ject might be attained. In the same way the Liberal Untonists were prepared to sink their political Was in presence of maintaining the Uuion. He had never disguised his opinion that recourse to the Crimes Act would be necessary after Mr. Gladstone had thrown dowa the bribe of Home Rule to Irish disaffection. Such a measure was required to put down the intimidation and tyranny of the National League. There was no room is the British Empire for two Governments and two execu- tives. Mr. Parnell and his friends have never disowned the policy of "public Plunder" Mr. Gladstone attributed to L them at Leeds Eve years ago; yet he now made them his 'allies.

Granted that prices have a tendency to find their working average as between master and man, it is still possible, in such an exceptional case as this, that a strike may be beneficial. Where is the political economist who will venture to say that it is a normal state of things for wages to fall as much as fifty per, cent ? It is ovident that the Chain- ' makers have submitted to monstrous ex- action. • because they were weak and were an easy prey in the hands of grasping em- ployers. A strike, long-continued as this has been, and supported, too, as it is by public opinion and subscriptions, will most likely be a lesson to unscrupulous masters which they will not readily forget. They will be forced to the conclusion that it does not pay e'ther to kill or starve the goose that lays the golden eggs; and will, perhaps, be content for the future to demand no more in the way of a re- duction in wages than is warranted by the fall in prices of • the manufactured article. But to make the most of the opportunity to be gained by the strike, the Chainmakers should organise ; they should join their Trades Union, recognising that "United they stand; divided they fall." They have been beaten almost out of existence by fighting single- handed ; let them stand shoulder to shoulder in the struggle, and they will then hold their own.

IT is pleasant to turn aside from the rush and roar of life in the nineteenth century to the records which history gives us of the slow and sleepy way in which our forefatheis jogged along in the days that are no more.. We pride ourselves on travel by express trains and communication by telegraph and 'telephone ; and certainly get through a great deal of business in a very little time; but, for all that, the questions will crop up—Whither? and Why ? The answer is not always satis- factory; and when, in the hot pace, limbs are weakened and nerves are shattered ere old age may be said to have arrived, it becomes pertinent to ir quire whether the race is worth the struggle. We have been led into this train of thought by dipping into the pages of the " History of Runcorn, with an Account of the Ancient Village of Weston, by Charles Nickson." It is a goodly quarto volume of over two hundred pages, which have been neatly printed on toned paper by. Messrs. Mackie and Co. A history of this kind is especially interesting, for when the record is of a place which is really ancient the reader is permitted to wan- der back in thought from century to century; and he gets glimpses of the continuity of habits and cus' oms which he could not other- wise obtain. Runcorn can boast of great age if not of great growth ; and it is therefore fitting that we should have the story of its life from year to year, This task Mr. NICK- SoN has taken upon himself ; and, labouring hard and conscientiously upon all the material he has been able to get together, he has issued a book which is invaluable as a work of reference. Turning to its pages, we find ourselves carried as far back as the year 76, when, it is stated, " a tribe of people. called the Ceangi or Cangi, lived in Cheshire," and roamed among "the woods that grew by the side of the marshy tracts extending for miles along the shores of the Mersey, by Norton, Runcorn, and Frodsham." Rumcaan was the ancient title of the place ; and there have been numerous learned and ingenious conjectures as to the origin of the name, though it cannot be said that the antiquarians have left the matter any clearer than they found it. It is by degrees, of course, that the spelling has been changed, passing through Runkhorne before settling down to Runcorn, just as the bottle of " oyle " in the parish church ac• counts for 1715 becomes "oil "at the present I time. There have been changes in other things besides spelling. "A Tourist's Guide to Runcorn " is not to be found now, except in museums, for, although there is still plenty of water at Runcorn it can no longer be de- scribed as "a watering place." A great many things have happened since the war- like Princess Ethelfleda built Runcorn Castle in 915 ; and amongst other things must be reckoned the disappearance of the castle itself, the last traces of it being swept away when the London and North-Western Rail- way Company laid the foundations of the magnificent structure which now spans the Mersey at Runcorn Gap. It is thus that the old order changes and gives place to the new. As might be expected, the Parish Church figures prominently in the history of Runcorn. The reader will find much to instruct him in the details which Mr. NICKSON has compiled and collated from various sources. The epitaphs which Are to be found in the church- yard occupy several pages of the volume ; but we have not space for more than two. One runs : She was young, and so are the flowers That fade with the summer away; And her memory is sweet as the showers That freshen the roses of May. The thought here is genuinely poetical, and so, too, is the form of expression. Roses in June or July would have been more strictly correct; but then what of the rhyme ? The other epitaph has the soul of wit, in that it is brief, and is as follows : Praises on tombs are trifles vainly spent; A man's good name is his best monument. The History, it may be added, deals at some length with the BROOKE family of Norton, several generations of whom are interred at the Runcorn Parish Church. There is one feature of the work which deserves to be specially commended, and that is that it is profusely and admirably illustrated. At page 167 there is'a reproduction from an old print of a "View of Runcorn in 184. o." It is very striking, but it is just a little too suggestive of miles of water at the sea side. The rest of the illustrations are from drawings by Mr. HEDLEY FITTON, of. Runcorn, who has a growing reputation as an artist. Amongst the more noteworthy of these must be men- tioned "Higher Runcorn," which makes a charming frontispiece, Runcorn Bridge, Run- corn Pier, Waterloo Bridge, Old Baths, the Parish Church, Holloway, and Waterloo-road. Mr. FITTON takes an artist's license in his canal views; but, as he has added rather than taken from the breadth and beauty of the canal, he may be pardoned. As an example of what he can do with simple material, we commend the view of Waterloo-road ; it is accurate, as the illustrations are as a whole. and yet it is made to look exceedingly pic- turesque. Mr. FITTON has had his heart in sketching as much as Mr. Nrciesoie has had in writing, and the result is a History of Run- corn of which Runcorn may be proud.

THE Government Coercion Bill is being forced through the House of Commons with ruthless determination, but not without such strong protest from the nation as will bear fruit at the next election. We are glad to think that the Liberals of this part of the country have done their duty in denouncing the last and worst proposal to apply "the ever

The de- monstration at Warrington, on Saturday evening, was as enthusiastic as it was large. It was ' known that Mr. JOHN CROSFIELD could not be present, and an admirable sub- stitute was found in Mr. WILLIAM CROSFIELD, who, as will be seen from our report of the proceedings, made a thoughtful and most effective speech. The absence of Mr. MC- MINNIEs was, however, a disappointment which was the more felt from the knowledge that nothing but illness of a severe kind would have prevented him occupying the chair as president of .lAe Warrington Liberal Association. In otheflespects the meeting was fortunate, for in addition to Mr. W. CROSFIELD, MT. NEVILLE, M.P., and Mr. ARTHUR O'CorrNoa, M.P., attended and de- livered addresses which roused the feeling of the audience to the highest pitch in pro- testing against the .injustice that was being done to Ireland by inflicting on her " a causeless and insulting Coer- cion Bill." The Working men's Committee who are engaged in agitating for the freeing of the r, Warrington Lending Library are showing themselves energetic and persistent. They are now getting a memorial signed to be presented to the Town Council with the object of inducing their representatives to defer the adoption of the unfavourable re- port of the Library and Museum Committee. They have but to fight the battle out on the present lines, and they will win/ They have got the franchise, and when the time comes they must, if the need arises, be ready to use it.

A youth named William Hulme was brought before the St. Helens magistrate, on Mon- day, for setting fire to gr4s on the banks of the reservoir belonging to the Liverpooi Cor- poration. If he who makes two blades of grass grow where only one grew before is a benefactor to his species, it follows that a de- stroyer of grass deserves severe punishment. But the offender in question was discharged with a caution. It was stated that he was not "all there," which must not be taken to mean that he proved an alibi for he was very much " there " when the grass was fired—but that he. wasn't quite responsible for his ;actions. Let boys who are '.all there" take warning.

growing keener and hotter; but the Liberals, if they remain true to themselves, need not fear the result. Lord HARTINGTON has at last given the word for the Liberal Unionists to organise, and fight for their own hand. They have, of course, the right to do this; ;nit when they range themselves on the side of the enemy they must expect to be dealt with as enemies. We may regret that there should be great differences of opinion upon a great issue; and we are bound to respect con- scientious convictions ; but at the same time, believing as we do as Liberals that Home Rule is the true and only remedy for the grievances of Ireland, we rnust endeavour by all the legitimate •means in our power to overcome all opposition—whether it proceeds from stupid Tories, Liberal Unionists, or Radical Coercionists. This was the spirit in whiCh the meeting addressed itself to the Irish question on Saturday evening. It is recognised that the task is a great one; but the Liberals of the United Kingdom, having their hearts in the work, will go forward until Ireland shall be blessed with self- government, and coercion shall be known no more.

DASTARDLY ASSAULT ON A DITTON BOY: TILE . PRISONER COMMUTED. '

At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage, John Taylor, a man about 30 years of age, son of John Taylor, of the New Bank Farm, Cow-lane, Ditton, was brought up on remand charged with having on Tuesday the 20th ult , committed a robbery with violence upon Joseph Smith. 13 years of age, eon of the stationmastet at Ditton Junction Railway Station, and stolen a knife and trowel The prisoner was undefended. The evidence showed that - on the afternoon of the day in question the boy set out from home with the intention of gathering fern's. • He went along Ditton Bank for about a mile and a half. arid then turned to the right along the iitch side. Here be met the prisoner, and asked him if he could show him bnyrica•; ferns. The prisoner took him to a plantation en the fand• of Mr. Tharme. where there is a pond of water. Pointing' to something in the water the prisoner asked "What's that," and upon the boy looking in the direction indicated, the prisoner give hits a push and he fell into the water ; which. was about three' feet deep. By the aid of the overhanging brae-eh of a tree he got upon the bank, and attempted to shout, but the prisoner placed One hand over ths. hey'et month, and with the other seized his throat. The boy made. ineffectual struggles to release himself, and atlectb.l4o• prisoner loosened his grasp and kicked the boy on the c4ieek, again knocking him into the water. The boy was edranibt ling out a second time when the prisoner kicked him on the left ear, and through the force of the blow he agaitilep into the water. Having administered toe boy a fifrther kick on the head the prisoner departed: The boy waded out of the water and became unconsciiint: When re- covered Se missed his knife and trowel. On the war home he was very sick, and fell down several times ,throngh 01. banstion, and it was with great diffleultv he arrived,there. The water in the pit was stagnant and very dirty, and he swallowed a great quantityof it. To his evidence the boy said the prisoner appeared to be solder. and he wondered why he was doing ibises he had never given him any prove- cation.—Jos. Smith, stationmaster at Ditton Junction,depdsA that when his son arrived home his head was swollen as large again as its natural 5iZ3. Doe boy was more or lees covered with blood, which appeared to have flowed from a large cut on the left ear, and from a wound on the right side of the mouth. The boy had also a severe bruise behind the left ear. His neck was also very much swollen. and:there were marks of P thumb and fingers on his throat. The boy. was unconscious when he first saw him, and he was wet anal, cold from head to toot. A doctor- was sent for, eloct Dr. Richards arrived, and ordered the boy to bed, where he was confined for five days—Dr. MeCambridge descrito•d minutely the boys injuries, and said for two or, three days he was in great danger. Ha was not in a tit condition to leave thc house until eleven days after the occurrende.— P.C. Worthington stated that when 'he, apprehended the priioner, the latter said. "I shall get more this time than I L got last time," and after a pause he added. "I should never have done it, only I bad a sup of drink "—P.S. McGregor said at the police station he charged the prisoner with un-,' lawfully and maliciously wounding the boy and causing grevious bodily harm, and with endangering his life by,- throwing him into a pit. The prisoner made no reply, and he now had nothing to say. The mother of the prisoner, said he was not responsible for his actions,—The Bench committed the prisoner to takc his trial at the next iLiyer- pool Assizes. : . r
