div.p: "TOUCH AND GO."

It is reported that notice has been given of 136 amendments to the first clause of the Crimes Bill. It must be a wretched thing to need so much amending. Would it not be better if it could be improved out of existence?

Our Tory contemporary makes merry over the printing of Sir George Trevelyan's letter on Coercion, which it speaks of as "unread- able." We will not retort as we might, but simply say—" our withers are unrung" ; it was not printed at the office of this journal.

Osman Digna has as many lives as a cat He has been " killed " about half a dozen times; but he is again upon the scene. The latest report is that the Hadendowas have made a prisoner of him. He will soon be at liberty of course, and —" killed" again.

It fell upon a day In the merry month of May that the carters throughout the district made a goodly show with their gaily-decked horses, and gladdened the hearts of all who saw them. It is a capital thing to give prizes for the best turn-out on May Day. It is good for the men—it is a feather in their caps ; good for the horses—for they like to be well groomed; and good for everybody, since "a thing of beauty is a joy for ev.r."

At Runcorn, in addition to providing the usual treats, it has been resolved to cele- brate the Jubilee by erecting a Cottage Hos- pital. The motion was opposed by several working-men, who showed commendable regard for the independence and self-reliance of their order. But now that it has been de- cided to go on with the proposal, it is to be hoped that opposition will be converted into emulation in making the Hospital '1 credit to the town.

Mr. L. Gordon Rvlands was heartily wel- corned at the anti-coercion m3eting, at War- ringtbn, on Saturday evening, as the son of the late Mr. Peter Rylands. He made his debut in good style, on being called upon to move a vote of thanks to the speakers. It is to be hoped that, in the course of time, the Liberals of Warrington will have many oppor- qunities of moving a vote of thanks to him as an advocate of the Liberal cause.

The attempts which are being made to entrap the Irish members of the House of Commons are cowardly in the extreme. The Tories know that in the present state of pub- lic opinion it would be hardly possible to get an impartial jury in this country if action were taken against the " Times" for its slander- ous accusations ; and is just because they do know this that they seek to force the issue in this direction. They talk, too, about " honour" and -" fairness"; but they had better not use such words in such a connec- tion.

It has always been acknowledged that Mr. Dillon is straightforward and fearless ; but he is not such 'a fool as to play into the bands of the enemy. He is accused by the " Times " of making an explanation which is "a tissue of gross and palpable false- hoods ;" a Tory member refers to this as "a breach of privilege "—as it certainly is—and when Mr. Dillon shows himself willing to meet it as such, and even to go the length of sub- mitting the matter to a Select Committee of the House of Commons, the Government turn tail, It is no breach of privilege, it seems, to charge members of the House of Commons with deliberate falsehood. Lying is a privilege; it is one of the blessings of a "Salisbury" Government.

Mr. Chamberlain, in another quarter, gives countenance to the foul accusations against the Parnellites. On being cornered by Mr. John Morley, who reminds him that in 1885 he advised that Mr. Parnell, and other Irish leaders, should be taken into counsel by the Queen's Government, he tries to wriggle out by saying this was before the "Times" had made public what is called " the Parnell letter." But it won't do; the member for West Birmingham had proceeded to associate the Parnellites with assassins after 1885, and before the publication of the "Times' letter. He has changed front, and had better own it.

Ralph Bate. Of Runcorn has found, at the cost of 225 6d, that he cannot act in "the way they have in the army," even when he is in the "Salvation Army Citadel." In law the citadel is "a place of worship," and Ralph has had to appear before the magis- trates for bad behaviour therein. The Sal- vationists are not over-refined in their
LOCAL NE Y.

MOST PEOPLE ARE IGNORANT of the value of eyesight. In many. instances when they first find their eyesight fail- ing, they purchase all kinds of inferior manufactured spec- tacles which in the end cause their eyes to burn and ache. To remedy this defect, A. Freaks, of 95 and 97, Deansgate, Manchester, and 143, Lord-street, Southport, has invested his" Perfection " Spectacles, which be adopts at either of the above addresses at 7s 61 per pair. He will guarantee that they are not to he eqoalled in the cometry for clearness coolness, and rest they impart to the eyes. Pamphlet "How to preserve the sight " free on apolication.—Adet. MEASLES AT WlDNES.—Mtms'ss are very prevalent is the West Bank district of Widoes at the present time. The disease is not, however, of a very virulent nature, and no deaths have yet occurred. RUNCORN AND THE WHITSUNTIDE HOLIDAYS.—At meeting of the delegates of the various Dissenting Sunday Schools, on Wednesday night, it was decided that the usual procession of scholars should take place on Whit-Monday. A VAGRANT AT RUNCORN.—Xt ItanCOra Police Court, on Thursday, before • Captain Hazleburst, Al;ce Ham-son was charged with being drunk and sleeping in an outhouse in Grindroll square. The case was proved by P.C. Millington, and the prieener, who had only been released from gaol on the previous day, was sentenced to 14 days' hard labour.

Dons AT LARGE AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Fes• sions, on Monday, a fine ot 61 and costs 9s 6J, was imposed upon each of the following persons for disobeving an order of the magistrates by allowing their dogs to be at large.— J. 0. Jackson, grocer, Bridge-street; T. Clough, butcher, Church-street; S. Cex C trcer, Yerk-street ; aud S White, Se wel I. street. _

PRESENTATION AT WIDNES. - Mr. S. Drought, of Frederick-st., who has recently resigned the position of superintendent to Simms Cross Primitive Methodist School, after seven years service, was presented with a handsome writing desk the other evening as a taken of the esteem and appreciation in which he is held by the teaching staff of the se. 001. Mr. S. Owen, the present superintendent, made the presentetion on behalf of the subscribers, and Mr. 1, Drought suitably acknowledged the gift. RENOVATION OF AN OLD FARMHOUSE AT RUNCORN.- Pool Farm, at present occupied by Mr. S. Partington, and owned by Mrs. C. Hazlehurst, of the Grange, is under. going a precess of renovation. The house is one of the oldest and quaintest in Runcorn. Standing back a few yards from Heat-la-road, Mid overlooking the Big Pool from which it takes its name, the dwelling its a hall timbered one of the seventeenth century, with a low slated roof and small windows. In front of the house was a date stone with some curiove characters, and A date denoting that the house was erected in 1689. The present improvements were ren. dered necessary owing to the fact that the walle of the building threatened to collapse. trnees bTARR BowIKETT BUILDING SOCIETIES.-A meeting under the auspices of the first and second Starr *Bowkett Building Societies, was held in the Methodist Free Church, on Tuesday night. Dr. McDonnell presided, and there was a fair attendance. The Chairman delivered an I address on the advantages of the societies, and Mr. T. 8.1 Swale also spoke in a similar vein. Songs were given by Miss Kilsall, Mr. Finn, and Master C. H. Bate, and Mr. Punter gave recitations. The chief attraction was a couple of appropriations, by which Mr. Win. Wilcocks became en- titled to £2OO free of interest for 12i years, and another member whose name has not been revealed (No. 158) be- came entitled to .£4OO a year on similar terms. RESCUE FROM DROWNING AT RUNCORN. - TbORHIS Roach, a clogger, employed at the shop of Mr. Page, Bridge- street, performed a courageous deed on Monday. During / the evening a little girl named Martin, who lives with her ; parents in Stone-street, fell into the canal. Several persons I ' assembled and tried to reach the girl with a prop, but their efforts were not successful. Roach, attracted to the spot by the shouts of the persons present, without a moment's hesi- tation jumped into the water, and rescued the girl, who was then unconscious and apparently dead. Mr. Isaac Speak- man, chemist, was sent for when the child was taken home, i and under his direction consciousness was restored. Dr.j McDougall afterwards attended the child. We learu that this is the second life Roach has saved, and his bravery I certainly merits the notice of the Humane Society. DISTURBING THE SALVATION ARMY AT RUNCORN.-Be. fore Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. G. L. Davies, at Run- corn Petty Sessions. on Monday, Ralph Bate, a young man, was charged with having on the 24th April been guilty of unlawful, riotoue, violent, or indecent behaviour in a cer- tain place of worship called "The Salvation Army Citadel."l The defendant pleaded not guilty. Joseph Matthews, the hall keeper, put in the certificate of registration of the building as a place of worship, and John Williarnsog, a sawyer, Annie Rogerson, of Dover-street, and Maggie Beech, captain of the Runcorn Branch of the Army, gave ' evidence as to the defendant's conduct. It appeared that during the afternoon service the defendant continually made remarks of an obscure nature, causing considerable disturbance amongst those present. He was asked to leave, and a hymn Was sung. to give him a favourable opportunity, but he still remained; and asked to be put out. The aid of the police was invoked, and P.S. Woolley and P.C. Suther- land, patting in an appearance, the defendant departed. A fine of 10a, and costs 12a 6d, was imposed. MAY DAY PROCESSION AT WIDNES -The advent of the merrie month of Sewers was celebrated in Widnes on Mon- day. Under the auspices of the May Day Procession As- sociation of which Mr. C Edwards-Moss, M.P. is the patron. the Bth annual procession of horses and vehicles of various descriptions took place. The animals were gaily decked with ribbons; of every hue, and as they proceeded through the main thoroughfares of the town, headed by the Ditton Brass Band, they were viewed by large numbers of spectators. Previously to the display, however, there was a competition for a number of prises off-red by the Association, for which there were about 36 entries. The judges were Messrs John Kenwright, Tarbuck Hall ; Win. Turton, Burnt Mill Farm, Hate; and William Johnson, Old Hall, Bold, and their awards for the bet, neatest, and cleanest turnouts were as follows :-Class 1, manufacturers' double draught horses: 1, William Smith: ironfounder ; 2 Messrs. Muspratt and Sons. Class 2, manufacturers' single. draught horses: 1, Widnes Local Board; 2 and 3, Mr. Peter Longton, brewer, Dirton. In class 7, contractors' and cart owners' double cobs, there were no entries. Class 8, contractors' and cart owners' single cobs: 1, James Hulme, 2, John Valentine, 3, J Hemingway. Class 9, business and private turnouts of traps: 1, S Sadler, 2, H Herriman, 3 Thomas Gerrard. Class 10, business turnouts of spring carts, van, &c., 13 hands and over: 1, R Woods, 2, S Sadler, 3. THE OUTBREAK OF ANTHRAX.-The Chief Con- stable of Cheshire announced on Tuesday that the anthrax outbreak on the farm of Messrs Percival, at Aston, had been stamped out. The outbreak has, however, cost Messrs Percival the loss of just 100 head of stock of various descriptions. Swine fever prevails to a great extent, 53 animals having been attacked during the past week, against 70 during the previous week. LETTER FROM Mn. GIADSTONE.-Mr. GI W. Rawlins has received the following letter, in ac- knowledgment of the resolution passed at the Earlestown meeting on Saturday, 23rd April, and forwarded to Mr. Gladstone :-" House of Commons, 4th May, 1887.-Sir,-I am desired by Mr. Gladstone to acknowledge with his cordial thanks the receipt of the resolution which" you have done him the honour to transmit to him on behalf of the Earles- town meeting.-I am, sir, your obedient servant, G. W. SPENCER LvrrLEToN. Gerald W. Rawliis, Esq."

div.head: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.
div.p: HEALTH OF THE TOWN.

The Medical OffiCe-r---re-pOTte-d---ih-a-t the number of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 25. Four deaths were due to heart disease, three to consumption, four to inflammation of the lining membrane of the brain, two to child birth, two to bronchitis, three to diseases of abdom- inial original, two to natural decay, and one each to convul- sions, erysipelas, blood disease, paralysis, and congestion of the lungs. The above 25 deaths showed an average death rate for the twelve months of a fraction over 18 per 1.000. He inspected the common lodging-bosses last week, and found some of them in a satisfactory condition ; others had to be reminded of the Anthony's requirements.

div.head: LAW CLERK.
div.p: THE LAW CLERK.

The Chairman said before they proceeded with the next business he should like to say how plete-d they were to see Mr. Linaker, the law clerk, returned from hizi tour. (Hear, hear.) He Was glad to find that he was very much better, and he hoped he would continue to improve in health and strength, and be prosperoua and We in the midst of his family for a long period of time. (Hear, hear.)—The :Law Clerk : I thank you, Mr. Chairman. FINANCE COlft ITTEE. •

This committee reported rh4t during the past month the receipts amounted to £3O ISs Id, and accouivs amounting to £205 184 2d were passed for payment. The tender of Mr. Renton Gibbs for alteration and addition to the heating apparatus r quired in connection with the new library premises, undertaking to do the work for £l7. WAS accepted. The tender of the Northern Assurance Company for the loan of .El7O at 4.4. per cent., repayable in 30 years, to defray the cost of extending the library, was also ac- cepted.

div.head: MR. W. J. SHORE AND THE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. . –
div.p: MR. W. J. SHORE AND THE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. . -

The Secretary read a letter from Mr. W. J. Shore resign- ing his position as a member of the Library Committee. It was, be said, with regret that be terminated his connection with genial work and agreeable colleagnes.—Mr. Lake said he had great pleasure in testifying to the Work Mr. Shore had done on the committee. He had het n a most regular and punctual member, and certainly one of the most useful members of the committee, and especially on the book Selection Committee, and they all regretted the loss of his presence. It was important that the ',oniony should be filled up at once, because the committee were preparing the estimate for the coming year, and there was much work to do in arranging and furnishing the new library premises, and he begged to propose as a fit and proper person to be a member of the committee, the Rev. A. Maitland Wood. His scholarship, his position, and the interest he took in all educational matters were a guarantee that he would make an admirable member of the committee.—Mr. Hankin- son seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.

div.head: L COMPLIMENT.
div.p: L COMPLIMENT.

At the close of the business, the Chairman, Mr Lake, and Mr Dobson referred to the fact that Mr C Nickson, of the "Runcorn Guardian," would in the coarse of a week take a position at Aitrincham similar to that he had occupied at Runcorn, and complimented him on the fairness with which he had represented the proceedings of the Board to the public, and the accurate manner in which all their business had been reported.—Mr Nickson, in acknowledging the kind expressions of the members, said that though his duties at the Board had sometimes been of an arddoas character, they had been rendered agreeable by the kindly spirit invariably displayed by each member.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
The mcntbly meeting was held at the To ffn Waterloo.road, on Tuesday night. Present : Mr. J. Pritchard (chairman), Dr. McDongill, Messrs.. S.. C. Beckett, F. A. Lake, and G. Moss (clerk.)
THE NEW CLERK.

Mr. Moss said : Mr. Chairman, before I proceed further to read the minutes, perhaps I may be allowed to thank the Board ter the honour they have conferred upon me in electing me clerk. I hope in the future to justify the ap- pointment they have made.

div.head: RETIRING CLERK.
div.p: THE RETIRING CLERK.

The Chairman said he would take that opportanity of re- ferring to the services of their late clerk, Mr. F. Rigbv. Mr. Rigby wa-, the first clerk that wa3 appointed by the -Board, and he had held the position for 12 years. He (the chair- man) had had the honour of sitting at the Board during that period of time, and he could testify to the great ability which Mr. Rigby lead shown in the administration of the work of the Board. He had a most perfect knowledge of the Education Acts, and when the Board had occasion to appeal to him to elucidate any intricate subject, be had al- ways done so with skill and judgment. Being the first clerk to the Board Mr. Rigby had to formulate and adopt a system for carrying oat its work, and recently he had a great deal to do in carrying out an arrangement for the building and opening of the new schools and in negotiating the loans for the erection of the same. He had often ad- mired the tone and diction of his official communications to the Educational Department, and what they considered of them might be gathered from the promptitude by which they were attended to by my lords. He might say further, that the Board had no surcharges.during that period to con- tend with, and he (the chairman) considered that Mr. Rigby had carried out with much ability the duties of the clerk- ship, and he had left to his successor a system which would greatly help him in understanding the business of the Board. •

div.head: QUERN'S XUICILNE._
div.p: THE QUERN'S XUICILNE._

The Clerk read a circular letter issued from the London School Board, asking the Runcorn School Board to join in presenting an address to the Queen congratulating Her Majesty upon the progress made in the work of public educa- tion during the 50 years of her reign. A draft addressaccom- panied the letter.—Mr Lake: I don't see any special reason why we should join, but still I don't see anything to object to. 'The address merely recites certain facts during lier Majesty's reign with regard to education. I suppose the facie are beyond dispute—Dr McDougall said the address seemed to him to be a rather too ponderous document to put their signatures to it without having gone carefully through it. However willing the London Board might be to dietin- guish themselves, he would rather see a county memorial to Her Majesty conducted very much upon the lineof Tubileead- dresses generally_ It seemed to him thatihe London School Board had not set the best example for countrY schools intha district, and he should object himself to putting any signs- t nreto that document, simply at the dictation of the London School Board.—Mr Lake: It is merely an Invitatien' and the address does not confer any approval upon the London School Board. It is merely congratulating Her Majesty upon the improvement made in education during her reign. That is the long and short of iL—The Clerk t We are not asked to sign the address now. It will be referred to us at, later day.—Dr McDougall: It will be better to 'clefs, the question, so that every person could consider whether he could honestly put his name to it—The Chair- man Pass k round after the meeting.—Mr Lake: I have seen enough of it to satisfy me there is no harm in it.—The rattler was then adjourned.

div.head: – – THE ASSISTANT VISITOR.
div.p: - - THE ASSISTANT VISITOR.
Mr George lio—w—ar.d—, one of the visitors. applied for an increase of salary. Elia application was referred to the School Attendance Committee.
_ THE etrARDIANS AND THE PAYMENT OP SCHOOL FEES.

_ The Visitor (Mr. Bowyer) presented a report in which he stated that threugh the sedan of the school fees inquiry officer of the Board of Guardians (Mr. Ward), in refusing the payment of fees to indigent person., conside.—ble diffi- culty had been caused both to parents of children, who F should attend to voluntary schools, and to the visitors. Applications for fees were constantly being made to the visitors, who were unable to pay fees through poyeety,'and through the action of the isquiry officer, the fees ins great many deserving cases were unpaid, and children were even refused admission to school, and at any rate attended irre- gularlv.—Mr. Beckett said this was a very awkward mat- ter. It was really injurious to the managers of the schools, and he thought that some steps should be taken.— Dr. McDougall asked was it not more injurious p the school children. The Board Schools did not admit of any teaching beyond the 2od standard, and theref.re all chi'. dren between the 2nd and 6th standards had to attend voluntary schools, and if the parents were not in a position to pay fe-s, those children were not admitted. Conse- quently they were left uneducated, and not having passed the requisite standards, could not aid their parents in the manner they ought to be able to do. It seemed to hum a very curious and peculiar action for the Board of Guardians to refuse the payment of fees. The fees would be paid out

div.p: ANTI-COERCION DEMONSTRATION AT WARRINGTON. SPBBCHES BY Mu. Nuirm.l.P. Mu. A. O'Cormort.. M.P., and Mu. W. CNSFIELD. On Saturday evening a mass meeting of Liberals was held in the Public Hall, at Warrington, in con- demnation of the Coercion Bill. The hall was crowded, and a resolution of protest was carried amid much enthusiasm. The chair was occupied by Councilor F. A. Roberts, and amongst those also present on. the platform were Mr. Neville, M.P. (Exchange Division of Liverpool), Mr. Arthur O'Connor, M.P., (Donegal), Mr. W. Crosfield (Liver- pool), the Revs. G E Cutting, R Filcher, 8.A., A Kenworthy, J Calvert, and Weaver; Drs. J H Gor- nall, J.P., and Geary ; and Messrs. John Greening, J.P., C S Burgess, J H Fleming, E J Guest, J.P., John Brown, William Pierpoint, L G Rylands, G W Rawlings (Rainhill), Peter Caldwell, George Black- burst, Thomas Birchall, F Loughlin, Arthur Brown, Ernest Lees, James Woods, Claud J Morris, Thomas Hall, James Strange, P M Campbell, Michael Cham- bers, Isaac J Biddle, Wm Mullard, George Clay, Thos Flood, Samuelßarlow, A H Corney, William Stirrup, Charles Sudlow, Benjamin Farrar, Joseph Dolan, Joseph Albinson, Edward Wallington,. James Boer' cock, John Chalmers, William Hayes, junr., Herbert Richards, Samuel Dunn, John Henry Norburyoßich- ard Siddall, Charles Longshaw, DavidHooley,Elisha Wallington, William Longshaw, Caleb Cardus, Eli- jah Ford, P T Winskill, John Griffiths, Edward Whithead, James Summersgill, David Tinnion, Ed- ward Twiss, John Bromley, David Wood, Alexander Blackhurst, James McGarty, John Edwin Richard- son, David Davies, William Ford, George Walker, Thomas Miller, John Mullins, John Jackson, Joseph Owen, John Wesley Harvard, John Williams, Wil- liam Twiss, Joseph Harrison, Thomas Mather, Jas. McClew, H E Roscollor, Peter Clare, Samuel Dun- bobbin, Alfred Webster, Thomas Trow, Joseph , Monks, Charles Plinston, Joseph Bunch, Bernard Percival, Edward Fenton, John McConville, John Barker, James L3rness, William Gilbert, John Kean; and H Roberts (Secretary of the Liberal As- sociation.) Before the meeting commenced Mr. H. Ronzurs, secretary, read letters that had been received from gentlemen who were unable to attend. Mr. Mc- Hinnies, J,P., wrote:—" I regret exceedingly that the state of my health will not permit me to be present at the Liberal meeting to-night. I should be glad to have borne my testimony against the unjustifiable measure of Coercion proposed by Government. I consider this measure an insult to the Irish nation, and calculated to estrange them from their British fellow-subjects, and prevent that real union between the two countries which is so . desirable in the interests of both. I hope your meeting will be a great success, and will be one more powerful protest against this great injustice." (Cheers.) Mr. John Crosfield, writing from Torquay, said;—" I am very sorry that it is utterly impos- sible for me to be present at your meeting on Satur- day night. I consider the Coercion Bill of the Tory Government cruel, wicked, and unnecessary. Had I been able to be with you on Saturday, I would have denounced this Toiy Government, and their measure in the strongest language I could com- mand. I trust you will have a large and enthusiastic meeting, and that your resolution con- demning this weak and miserable Government will be carried unanimously." Mr. John Rylands. in a letter, remarked that there was much to be said on both sides about Home Rule, but he could not under- stand Liberals voting for the proposed Coercion Bill; and the Rev. R. P. Corlett, on behalf of the Catholie clergy of Buttermarket-street, expressed their regret that as Saturday was an inconvenient night they could not be present. The Rev. Father Browne. in a letter, observed that the meeting would certainly proclaim with no uncertain voice that the people of Warrington condemn the useless and insulting bill now before the country. The Rev. Father Thomp- son wrote that he could not but regret the measure as a studied incitement to crime. He trusted that Ireland-would, in spite of gross provocation, show 'the forbearance which Mr. Parnell had counselled, and that they would not by any word or act in- crease the difficulties which Mr. Gladstone had resolved upon overcoming. Letters had also been received from Mr. Z. .Armitage, J.P., Mr. J. P. Reynolds, the Rev. G. E. Yonng, and Mr. C. H. Broadbent. Mr. Mahoney, M.P., and Mr. Deasy, M.P., who had been expected to speak at the meet- ing were not, Mr. Roberts explained, able to be pre- sent. The CPLIIIIMiN, who was received with cheers, referred to the letters read by Mr. Roberts, first and fpremost of which, he said, was the apology from the gentleman who should have presided over the meeting. They in Warrington looked upon Mr. McMinnies as their "Grand Old Man." In Mr. Gladstone—(cheers)—they had a national "Grand Old Man," and in Mr. McMinnies a local one. (Cheers.) It was with sincere regret that they heard that Mr. McMinnies was unable to be present. He (the chairman) believed that the Liberals of Warrington were decided on the question they had met to consider. Ile believed that they were, heart and soul, opposed to the Coercion Bill— (cheers)—and that the meeting would be a reflex of a recent meeting of the Liberal Council, at which, by a unanimous vote, a resolution almost identical with the one that would be proposed that night was passed. It was, however, thought advisable that a wider voice should go from Warrington, and that the resolution should be submitted to a larger meeting. Tory friends had told them that they were too late in the field. Well, they did not ex- pect that they could prevent the passing of the; Coercion Bill, but they could still say that it was an unjust measure, and that they were determined to express their opinions on it. The meeting would be addressed by Mr. Neville—(cheers)—by Mr. Arthur Connor, an old and valued member of the Irish Nationalist party—(cheers)=-and by Mr. William Crosfield—(cheers)—and for these gentle- men he asked a patient hearing. (Cheers.) Mr. Navrixis, M.P., was the first speaker, and he was received with loud cheers. Having thanked the large gathering for their cordial reception of him, he proposed the following resolution in the absolute certainty, he remarked, that it would be passed :—" That this meeting, as representing the Liberal party in Warrington, is of opinion that the Government have shown no reasonable grounds for the application of further repressive legislation to the Irish people, and, believing also that the true remedy for Irish discontent cannot be found in coercion, but rather in a wise and just extension of the power of self-government, such as has been propounded by Mr. Gladstone, emphatically de- nounces the new Coercion Bill as an unjustifi- able and base attempt to rivet the fetters of a cruel bondage upon our fellow subjects." (Cheers.) His (Mr. Neville's) first step in political life was when he determined to throw himself heart aad soul into the contest they had been waging on be- half of the liberties of the Irish people. He was going to say that he was a Home Ruler before Mr.l Gladstone, but he did not think that would be true. He was a Home Ruler before Mr. Gladstone lent the incentive of his great name to the movement, but he did not suppose he was a Home Ruler before Mr. Gladstone in his heart was. No time or labour spent in this cause should he think wasted, for the greatest satisfaction life could possibly give bias would be in the thought that he had had some share in settling those difficulties which had existed for so many years between the English and the Irish peoples, which had been so fatal to the interests of one country, so prejudicial to the interests of the other. Both at the general election and at the bye-election in Liverpool he asked those whom he was addressing what they proposed to do if they did not help Mr. Gladstone to pass his measure. It seemed to him that there was only one alternative. If they did not meet the wishes of the Irish people, and leave to them the management of their own internal affairs, the only remain- ing resource was absolute repression of Irish feeling and sentiment. For 86 years England had tried to govern Ire- land and had miserably failed—(cheers)—and now the question of what was to be done with Ireland was again tieing them. Would they meet the just requirements of , the Irish people, or go on in the old way. They could not I expect the latter to succeed, and nothing remained now bat to deprive Ireland of every vestige of liberty—to govern it absolutely or not at all. The Tories and the Liberal Unionists at the last election said that was not true. They said," Put power into our hands, and we will show you bow we can succeed in governing Ireland by the ordinary law, and in restoring peace and contentment to that country without resorting to stringent measures, and without meet- ing the demand of the Irish for self-government." The country, as far as one could judge, accepted that view of the case by returning the Tories and the Literal Unionists by a large majority to the House of Commons. Ever since that moment they had maintained that they had received from the country a definite mandate to maittiin the union between England and Ireland. Perhaps so, but they re- ceived no mandate to pat into effect those measures which he and those who thought with him, had said would be ab- solutely necessary if the wishes of the Irish people were not met. The Tories and Unionists had now proved as far as they could the truth of the assertions made by Liberals, that they could not govern Ireland under the ordinary law, by bringing in this Coercion Act. The Tories talked about maintaining the union, but he held that at the last general election there were no men in the country whose minds were so set upon preserving the union between England and Ire- land as the Gladstonian Liberals—(cheers)—except, per. baps, it were the Irish members themselves. Now that the union was threatened, it was their duty to look round and find a cause, and if possible, a remedy. After eighty-six Years of rule, based on the Act of Union,

(Hear, hear.) The Coercion Bill, Mr. O'Connor pointed out, created crimes which had never hitherto been kncwn to the law, and some of its provisions, as Sir George Trevelyan had pointed out, were directed not against crime but against political opoonente. (Hear, hear.) He then quoted a section from one of the Whiteboy Acts, and asked if any man in England could feel safe if Inch a provision were in force. The section read as follows :—" If any per- son or persoas shall knowingly send or deliver, or CAUSE, to be sent or delivered, any notice, direct or require any person to do or not to do any act, every person so offending shall be liable to transportation or imprisonment" ("Shame.") In the words of that section, if a person sent to his servant to ask her to get his lunch ready at twelve o'clock be would be liable to transportation or imprisooment. That is the kind of section, that is the kind of act, that is to be brought under the jurisdiction of resident magistrates. What kind of men were these resident magistrates? They belonged exclusively to one class. They were user-do-wells, and in most cases men who coald not get their liviog in any recognised profession. There was one man a notorious character in the South of Ireland who expressed himself on one occasion in these words: "We will fight the Nationalists to the death; we will fight them down to hell, and if hell is frozen over we will fight them on the ice." ("Shame." and laughter.) That was the kind of man who is at his own discretion to sentence or not to sealonce with or without hard labour for six months any person whom he chooses providing it can be said of that 'moon that he sent a message requesting or not requesting anyone to do or not to do "any act." ("Shams.") Mr. O'Connor then quoted statistics which went to show that relative to the population the number of crimes were much fewer in Ireland than in England; and he afterwards gave examples of exorbitant rackrenting on the part ef landowners. The object of this Coercion Bill, be said, was not to fight crime but to enable the landlords in this their eleventh hour, when they knew they must go, to carry with them as large a portions of spoil from the people of Ireland as they possibly can. (Cheers.) The resolution woe then put to the meeting and carried unanimously by loud acclamation. Mr. L. GORDON RYLAND% in rising to move a vote of thanks to the speakers, received a very cordial welcome. He thanked the audience for their kind reception, and said he had no doubt it was a recognition of the gallant services his late father bad rendered for political liberty. (Loud cheers.) They were all extremely pleased to make the acquaintance of Mr. O'Connor, and no doubt some of them were extremely surprised that he did not look at all like a brig-end or assassin. (Cheers and laughter.) Those who read the debates in the House of Commons must have come accost the foul charges continually being made against the Irish representative.. They would have seen them designated as ruffiane ; they would have seen them accused of associating with murderers, and of being privy to deeds of the darkest character, and of not only concealing, but of even aiding and abetting those deeds. It was somtimes said that It a mtn throws enough mud, some or it would stick, and it was perhaps not very surprising if some who heard those foul slanders continually repeated with unblushing hardi- hood might believe some of them. It was therefore in the highest degree desirable that the Irish members should come into contact with the English democracy. (Cheers.) The representatives of Ireland should come before English audiences. state their case, and defend themselves in person. They could explain their many great wrongs, and the Eng- lish people, in whom the lense of justice had always been strongly implanted, would, if they had justice on their side, and he believed they had, recognise and sympathise with them, and having in the past repeatedly sympathised with those who fought for op- pressed nationalities in all parts of the earth, they would at length turn their eves towards long-suffering Ireland and fight for the freedom of the Irish people. (Cheers.) That atrocious Bill they were met to protest against ought to be celled a bill for the better crushing of the liberties of the Irish people. (Cheers.) Mr. M. CHAMRERS seconded the vote of thanks, which was heartily accorded. Mr. O'Crnoron responded. and moved a similar compli- ment to the chairman, which was seconded by Mr. T. BIRCHALL. and carried. The meeting then terminated.

Secretarfes of Thotball Oluos are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be s sot tc the head office, Bewsey-street. Warrington, not later than ten o'clock an Wednesday morphia.
RUGBY RULES.

GLADSTONE-STREET STAR OF HOPE V. ALLEN•STREET ROVERS.—Played on the ground of the latter and resulted in an easy victory for the Star of Hope by two tries (ob- tained by Phillips) and 18 minors, to three minors. All played well for the winners. RUNCORN V. HALIFAX FREE WANDERERS.—The Runcorn team played their cloeing match for the season at Halifax on Saturday, and being minus Speakman, Cawley, and Wright, while the Wanderers bad the assistance of several members of the Halifax Club, the visitors were defeated by one goal (from a disputed try), a try, and one minor point, to a try and three minor points. FRODSRAM V. J. TUDOR'S TEAM.—Played RI Frodsham on Saturday. in the most pleasant weather. Frodsham won the toss, and played with the wind on their backs the first half. After some stubborn scrimmages, Barnes got over for Tudor's team rather easily, the kick at goal failing. Half-time was then called. On the change of ends Frod- sham had the superiority and finally' won by 2 goals 2 tries, and 9 minors to 1 try. The tries were got for Fred- sham as follows :—Webb, 2, W Tudor, 1 Thomas, 1. Barns at half-back, and Myers at three-quarter, played a good game for the visitors, while J Tudor, for the same, played a most splendid game, his runs creating exciting shouts of admiration from the spectators. For the home team Rod- gers played In his usual style. Webb, Tudor, and Darling- ton played a good game at three-quarters. Owen, at half- 'back played well, while the forwards one and all played a capital game. The umpires were GA Tudor, Weston, and W. Rodgers, Frodsham. J McWaters acted as referee.. WARRINGTON JUNIOR COMPETITION.

This competition has been continued during the present week, and has now almost run through to its final stage, the only remaining match being that of to-day (Saturday), be- tween Warrington Hornets and Warrington 2nd team. It should be mentioned that the whole of the proceeds of this match will be given to charities. On Saturday afternoon last no fewer than three matches were played. The first, in which very much interest was manifested, was between Sankey let and Rangers Ist. At the opening of the game the Rangers pressed their opponents very severely, but the latter gradaally recovered ground, and towards the end bad the best of the game, and won by a goal and a minor to nil. The next contest was between the Warrington Wanderers and Dallam-lane Amateurs, in which the Wanderers won by a try and six minors to two minors. The remaining of Saturday's matches was between Warrington Hornets let and Latchford True Blues, this game having to be replayed owing to the winning point of the Hornets on the previous evening being considered doubtful. The insects, however, again proved themselves superior to their antagonists, and qualified for the semi-final. On Monday evening the Hor- nets again turned out, having this time to face their own 2nd team. The result of this match was evidently a foregone conclusion, the juniors of course succumbing to the seniors. The last contest in the third round was between Warrington 2nd and the Catholic United. The Catholics were altogether too slow and unpractised for their nimble opponents, and were, therefore, beaten rather severely. The semi-finals were entered upon on Wednesday evening, when the Wanderers met Warrington 2nd. The Wanderers were hard pressed from the commencement and were very rarely permitted to invade the ground of the 2nd team. In the end the Warrington 2nd won easily by three tries and a considerable number of miners to nil. On Thursday the contestants were Warrington Hornets let and Sankey lat.' More than usual interest was taken in this match, as San- key were very generally expected to make a strong bid for the medals, while on the other hand the Hornets were by no means without their admirers. At the opening of the game it seemed as though Sankey were going to prove themselves the victors of the evening, as by dashing play they pressed the Hornets back towards their line. The Hornets, however, are particularly strong in the forward department, and they managed to relieve without conceding anything, the fast play evidently telling upon Sankey. Afterwards the Hornets had the advantage, though the quickness and capital organisation of Sankey prevented them from gaining anything more than a minor before half time. After half time, however, the superior strength of the Hornets' forwards began to tell its tale, and, some tough scrimmaging having taken place, they obtained a try, from which a beautiful goal was kicked. Later on another try was secured by the Hornets, who eventually won, having nilled their opponents.

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The annual meeting of this Authority was held at the Workhouse, on Friday morning. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Jolley, Dar- hyshire, Owen, Gibson, Kilshall, Swinton, Grange, J. Houghton, Pennington, and W. Long and Z. Ar- mitage (ex-officio) J. C. Sutton (clerk to the Guardians), Dr. Sal:42ton (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor), and F. Kerfoot (inspector). ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN AND VICE-CHAIRMAN. The CLERK intimated that the first businese of the Authority was the election of a chairman.—Mr. PENNINGTON moved that their late vice-chairman, the Rev. G. F. Roberts, be appointed chairman of the Authority. He thought that Mr. Roberts would fill the position as well as any one could do (Hear, hear.)—Mr. JoLLEY seconded, and Mr. DARBY. SHIRE supported this proposal, which was agreed to unani- mously.—On the motion of Mr. LONG, seconded by Mr. JOLLEY, sad supported by the CHAIRMAN, Mr. Darbvshire was appointed vice-chairman. PENKETH PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE.—This committee Was re-appointed with the exception of Messrs. Jeans and Ker- foot, whose names were left off on account of non-residence In the district. -

.—.—..-.. INCREASE OF SALARY.-11 was agreed that the salary of the medical officer should be increased from £6O to £BO, in consequence of the additional duties which would fall upon him through having to inspect the dairies and milk. shops of the district. SURVEYOR'S REPORT.—Mr. OWEN reported that since the last meeting the following inspections had been made : The Penketh Tanning Co.'s new shed, Penketh; Messrs. Taylor and Craik's houses, Manchester-road; Mr. Milling- ton's houses at Penketh, and the Wesleyan schools, Pen- keth. The following plena for new buildings had been submitted, and might be approved subject to the endorse- ments of certificates; Penketh Tanning Co., new abed; Mr. Bramball, four houses near to Wash-lane, Latchford, sub- ject to the cesspool being bailt where required; Mr. Grim- shaw's house in Grappenhall ; Mr. Thornton, two houses, Poulton-with-Fearnhead, subject to endorsement on certifi- cate as to drainage; Mr. Joseph mounfield, six houses in Manchester-road; and Mr. John Smith, jun., house in Grap- penhall.—The report was adopted. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—Dr. SEPFITON reported that the births for the month ending April 30th were males 27, females 24; deaths, males 16, females 7. The death rite from all causes was equal to 191 per 1,000, against 18 in the corresponding month of last year. The epidemic of measles at Hollins Green and Glazebrook had almost passed away. Most of the cases were convalescent, and he had not heard of any further attacks. ,The cases of typhoid fever at Penketh, reported at the last meeting of the Board, were almost well, but a further outbreak had occurred at one house, and bad proved fatal. There were also three cases at Cuerdlev. He had given instructions to the inspector to take certain sanitary precautions. This Was all the business.

COMBIITTEE.

The annual meeting of this committee was held at the Workhouse on Friday morning. There were pre- sent the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. J. Rylands, Z. Armitage, and W. Long (ex-officio), Blacktiurst, Pennington, J. Houghton, Balharry, and Ratcliffe ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and various assistant overseers.

ELECTION OF„ CHAIRMAN AND VICE•CHAIRMAN.—Mr. PENNINGTON moved at Mr. J. Ryiends be re-elected chairmAn.—This proposal was seconded by the Rev. G. F. ROBERTS, supported by Mr. Long, Mr. Derbyshire, and Mr. Z. Armitage, and agreed to.—The CHAIRMAN next moved that the Rey. G. F. Roberts be appointed vice-chairman, and Mr. J. HOUGHTON moved that Mr. Derbyshire be ap- pointed.—The Rev. G. F. ROBERTS seconded the latter pro• pesal, and withdrew his own nomination.—Mr. Darbyshire was then elected.

KtLuna's REPORT.—Mr. OWEN reported with regard to the Cheshire Lines Railway that, as instructed by the com- mittee at their last meeting, he had apportioned the in- creased assessment in the respective townships as follows, and bad given a copy of the figures to the Clerk :—War- rington, in borough, gross £2,010, rateable £1,675 ; War- rington, outside the borough, gross £645, rateable £537 10s; Poul ton-with -Fearnhead, £1,395 gross, rateable £1,162 103 ; Woolston - with - Martiescroft, gross £1,530, rateable £1,275; Itixton-witb-Glazebrook, gross £2,295, rateable £1,912 10s. These are calculated at £l,OOO per mile rateable value with one sixth added for gross annual value. Mr. Kenworthv, of Bank-street, appealed at the previous meeting against the assessment on the land he oc- cupies in Arpley. The assessments are in six items, and amount in the whole to gross £5B 53, rateable £54. Mr. Owen rented land from Lord Winmarleigh and Mr. T. H. Lyon. and pays £45 per annum, and £5 5s per annum to these owners rsspectively, making a total rent of £5O 5s for 26 statute acres of land. In his (the valuer's) opinion the assessment should be reduced to the rent, a portion of the land was untenanted for a year before. He had inspected the Theatre of Varieties, the assessment of which, grossl £llO, rateable £94, was appealed against at their previousl meeting by Mr. J. E.Wright. Mr.. Wright was just now ne- gotiating with a tenant, and was also considering the advi- sability of forming two shops out of the angles of the building fronting to Sankey-street. He (the valuer) there- fore proposed to leave the matter over, as an actual tenancy or tenancies might settle the question. With re- gard to the matter of reducing the assessment on the water supplied to the Corporation of St. Helens by the Collins Green Colliery Company, the valuer recommended that, looking at the facts, and 'also that the price for water will be still further reduced this year, it would appear that £350 might be a fair assessment, and that £250, as asked for, would be much more than a proportionate reduction.-- Adopted. div.p: to appeal against the assessment of their grounds at Hay- dock Park. The present assessment is £l,OOO grors, and £BOO rateable. Since the ground was formed, Mr. Stone said, the Company had made no profit in any single year, and the ground was also assessed above the rent paid. When the Company took the place the rent was fixed at £l,OOO a year, but it had been reduced to £BOO a year by Mr. Legh. It was thought at that time that the venture would prove sufficiently profitable to cover tbe £l,OOO a year, hut they had lost money each year. and there was no imme- diate prospect of the undertaking being succesqul. They considered that £BOO a year was still too high a rent, but as they had the ground on lease they had to take what they could get. He was of opinion that the agricultural value of the land was not more than £5OO a year. In answer to the Chairman, Mr. Stohe said that the ground was taken on a lease of 21 years from 1882. Since 1892 they had lost nearly £4.000. But no doubt, if things gere to get better. they would be glad to pay on a higher assessment.—Mr. BAIMARRY said be thought if the land was let at its agri- cultural value it would not bring in £5OO a year.—After some discussion it was resolved that the assessment of the ground should be reduced to £BOO gross, and £7OO rate- able. This was all the business of public interest.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING.
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING.

HERas.—The culture of these in gardens used to en- gage more attention when the residences of the wealthy had distilleries attached to them to extract the medicinal and aromatic properties from the herbs, but now that more potent rnedicinial plants of hotter climes are so easily and expeditiously produced, the culture of herbs is confined to those used for culinary purposes.—Mar. joram : Is used for soups and other dishes in first class cookery, and can only be disposed of at first class green- grocer shops. Its culture is very simple and consists in dividing the roots at this time and planting them one foot apart —Savoury : This requires similar treatment, but it is probably propagated oftener from seed sown now in a warm corner. Summer Savoury is an annual that may be sown now on a warm border, and the plants must be thinned.— Mint: The more the roots of this plant are cut about the better it seems to grow, and beds left undisturbed for years will grow weaker and weaker, and ultimately die out. We nearly lost it years ago in this way, and we set about making a new bed by taking up what roots we could find and placing them on the surface of a well manured piece of ground and covering them over three or four inches deep. The old bed was dug and manured to be in readiness for a crop of some other kind, but be- fore our intentions could be carried out pieces of mint growth appeared here and there, and by the end of the season it was, of the two, the best bed, obviously be- cause, in the operation of digging, the roots had been cut into numerous pieces, and each one be- came a plant. Since then we have improved beds by thrusting the spade into the ground a few inches distant and top-dressed with soil or a mixture of this and the contents of an old hot-bed.— Sage: This grows well in most soils, but by age the plants become "leggy," and are apt to die off, so that it is advisable to make a fresh plantation every two or three years. Propagation may be effected by seed sown now, or by slips taken off during the next two months and inserted in a shady border. Remove the lower leaves, or those on the portion that enters the soil. Water, if the soil is dry, at planting time. Thyme Should be sown every other year. It prefers dry, light, rich soil, and the seed, which must only be sparingly covered, may be sown in shallow drills or broadcast, and when the plants are large enough to thin, which will be in June or July, the surplus may be planted in rows six or eight inches distant. The plant may also be increased by slips and division of the .roots, but both methods occupy much more labour than seed-sowing, and, in our opinion, the plants are not so vigorous. THE FRONT GARDEN.—The rain which is descending _ . .

as we write, though cold, will work wonders in this as in other departments of the garden, and flowers that have been struggling to expand will rapidly develop. The following are in flower, but many of the blossoms look singed with the cold wind—auriculasop sorts, pul- minaria virginica, and officinalis. The latter is a well- known inhabitant of cottage gardens, and in some locali- ties by the common name lungwort. The plant has large spotted leaves, and the flowers are reddish-pink, borne in branched panicles. Muscavi (grape hyacinth), blue and white varieties, look pretty in groups with about a score of racemes in each. Hybrid primroses are beautiful and I interesting, and will soon make a grand show. Those who visited the spring show of the Preston and Fulwood Horticultural Society in March last will recollect the row of these that margined Mr. Troughton's group in front of 1 the orchestra, which we were informed were only taken 1 out of the open ground a few days before the show, and will have no dchibt formed some idea as to their value for pot culture as well as for the front garden. Narcissus of of sorts, hyacinths, wallflowers, anemones, arabis, and aubretias complete the list. THE GREENHOUSE—A light shade over the roof of this would be the means of prolonging the flowering period of many of the plants, as well as preventing scorching in others. A piece of thin canvas, or some of the materials manufactured especially for the purpose, stretched from one end of the house to the other, and over the part that requires shading ke most, might serve the present purpose. For a largAbouse pieces are usually stitched together, and one side is tacked on to a lath which is screwed to the upper part of the roof, and the other is attached to a roller with a grooved3wheel at one end, with a rope to draw up or let down. This arrangement , is far superior to all kinds of permanent shading, but if on some bright hot day the blind is forgotten and not let down much mischief is likely to occur, and it would have been as well if it had never been put up, so that for those who are not at all times near hand or troubled with a bad memory, some kind of permanent shading will be preferable. Whitening and water, sprayed on with a syringe or put on with a brush will remain on until washed off by the rain, and if a little boiled oil is added, it will adhere to the end of the season, and gives some trouble to remove if too much oil is used. Whitening and butter-milk mixed will also adhere until frost comes, and is readily moved. Ey adding a little green colour or washing blue the glaring whiteness is taken off.

The time of one of her Majesty's judges was taken up at Leeds Aslizes, on Thursday, by an action for breach of promise in which the plaintiff was an elderly widow and the defend- ant a man in his 74th year. The jury awarded the plaintiff a farthing, and the Judge refused to allow costs. The plain- tiff is a mill worker, earning lie per week. ST. HELENS CONSERVATIVES AND THE GOVERNMENT Mr. Seton-Karr, M.P., has received the following letters in reply to a resolution of confidence in the Government recently adopted at a Conservative meeting at St.Helens Foreign Office, April 24, 1861.—Dear sir,—l am much obliged to you for your letter, and very glad to receive so hearty an expression of sympathy with our great unionist struggle from the Conservative and Liberal Unionists of St. Helens. —Believe me, yours very truly (signed), SALISBURY —H. Seton-Karr, Esq."—" 10, Downing.street, Whitehall, April 26th, 1887,—Dear sir.—Mr. W. H. Smith desires me to ex- press his warm thanks to the members of the St. Helens Conservative Club and the Grand Habitation of the Prim- rose League for the loyal support of the Irish policy of her majesty's Government. Mr. Smith notices with much pleasure the allusion to the patriotism and devotion to the cause of the Union shown by the Liberal Unionists amp dear sir, yours faithfully, HENRY LOPES.—a. Seton-Karr, Esq., M.P."

WIT AND HUMOUR.

If the "milk standard" is lowered as • proposed will water rates be increased? A young lady, being asked by a rich bachelor, "If not yourself, who would you rather be?" replied sweetly and modestly, "Yours truly." ' "Wore you ever caught in a sudden squall ?" asked an old yatchsman of a worthy citizen. "Well, I should think so," was the reply, "I have helped to bring up eight babies." "I beg pardon," said the awkward youth, as he step- ped on the hem of her flowing robe. "Don't mention it," she replied sweetly. "All trains are occasionally stopped by cattle." At a wedding the other day one of the guests' who is a little absented-minded, observed gravely: "I have often remarked that there have been more women than men married this year. The way to be happy is to be good to other people. You want to do your level best to convince other people of this. It is well that they should make themselves happy by being good to you. Miss Jennie Gray, an energetic young woman v,ho works a 100-acre farm in Dakota, says she could work another just as large if the fellows who want to marry her would stop bothering her. He was a carpenter. He had lifted his hammer:to strike a nail. Did he strike? Not much. He paused, then returned the hammer to his box. The twelve o'clock whistle had blown. He was working by the day. Why do you stand with your hat off, Jones ?" "Well, you see, I have been on the Continent a good deal, and it is the custom there to stand bareheaded when a funeral is passing." "That isn't a funeral; that's the South-Western express!" • READY RBTORT.—Husband (irascibly): "We don't need that rug any more than a cat needs two tails. How often have I told you, my dear, never to buy anything because it's cheap ?" Wife (with the air of one who has got the better of the argument): "But it wasn't cheap, my love. It cost eight pounds." TEEN AND Now.—" How Styles have changed since I was a girl," said an old lady. "When I was young we used to wear our dresses up to the neck, and gloves with only one button. Now they wear the glove up to the neck and only one button on the dress.'' THEY NEED CATS.—The natives in Spain keep locusts in cages for the sake of their "music." These people stand in need of cats. Good, strong, musical cats is what they Want, cats who are fearless and tireless, and they will have no use for locusts or such small deer. Hs Gcrr OFF IN TlME.—Wife (on board a train bound for Niagara Falls(—" There are so many bridal couples about, dear, perhaps we may be taken for one." Hus- band—" No danger. A gentleman asked me a little while ago if I was your first or second husband." Wife —" What ! Where is he?" Husband—" He got off at the last station." ,

_ TO JUBILEE LOVERS. On a Jubilee stile sat a Jubilee youth, With a Jubilee pipe in his Jubilee mouth; On his Jubilee back was a Jubilee coat, And a Jubilee collar round his Jubilee throat. With this Jubilee youth was a Jubilee dog, Hunting Jubilee frogs in a Jubilee bog; On his Jubilee side sat a Jubilee sirl, On whose Jubilee head lay a Jubilee curl. In that Jubilee field was a Jubilee bull, Eating Jubilee turnips his hunger to lull; When that Jubilee youth asked that Jubilee miss From her Jubilee lips for a Jubilee kiss. As that Jubilee bull raised his Jubilee head, Saw her Jubilee hair was a Jubilee red, Flashed his Jubilee eyes, raised his Jubilee tail, Tossed the Jubilee lovers o'er the Jubilee rail.

Tin] BARBER'S Sroar:—An old Irishman occupied a barber's chair recently, and he was drowsy. His eyes could not be kept open, and his head rolled about and dropped over upon his shOulder and down upon his chest in a way that made shaving a difficult operation for the knight of the lather' and a dangerous one for the patient. Finally the barber said gently but firmly, "Look a-here, sir—l can't possibly shave you unless you hold up your head." To which the response was made with drowsy indifference, "Well, thin, coot my hair." FIRST PRINCIPLES OF THB Bus.—A celebrated minia- ture painter, who was usually bard up, sometimes con- sented to take a pupil to help to inflate the cash account, though much against his inclination. A wealthy gentle- man called at the studio one day and begged the artist to take his son, a young man of sixteen, as a pupil, pro- mising to pay handsomely for the instruction. The boy was admitted for the sake of the money it would bring; but, much to .the painter's disgust, it was discovered that he knew nothing of the first principles of drawing. The young man sat for half an hour on the first morning watching the master at work, much to the latter's an- noyance, and finally wentured to ask for something to do. "All right—all right !" the artist replied, going to a closet and returning with a pair of muddy boots and a blacking-brush, "Here—black these boots, young man; it will give you breadth." SURE TO BE WI/mi.—The following story is told of Murphy, the well-known almanac-maker who predicted the severest frost of the century. Once, when sojourning in the country, he set out one fine morning on an ex- cursion. After proceeding a short distance, he came across a farm-labourer, with whom he entered into con- versation. This man, on learning whither hewas bound, earnestly advised him to turn back home again, on the ground that he was safe to get wet through before he reached his destination. There was nothing whatever apparent to justify this confidently-made prediction, and Murphy, wholly discrediting it, resolved to push on. He had not however proceeded far before a tremendous storm broke with startling suddenness, and drenched him to the skin. His professional interest was at once aroused as to the method by which the labourer had been able to forecast this atmospheric change. Ac- cordinglyhe hastened back, and, having succeeded in finding his man, interrogated him on the subject. " Well,' replied the labourer, " I'll tell you how it was, sir. You see my master has an almanac by a fellow named Murphy in the kitchen, and, looking at it this morning, I saw that he had put down the weather for to-day as bright and fine. But he is suCh a confounded liar that directly I saw that I knew we should have rain." COOL THIEVERY—The coolness of London thieves while engaged in stealing and their tact in getting out of a surprise are illustrated by many anecdotes. The landlord of an hotel met, as he started to go up his own stairs, a man doming down backward with a feather-bed on his shoulders. "What have you there," asked the• landlord. "A bed for you, sir," answered the man. "Nonsense—it is not for me! I have not ordered my bed." "No. 22, Dash Square, sir." "Au, I thought so! It's next door." The man turned, and bore the bed off before the landlord's eyes, who did not discover his loss until too late. The proprietor of another hotel was robbed one day in the most barefaced way. A man with a paper cap on his head and a white apron round his body made his appearance in the coffee-room, where many guests were lunching. Looking intently at the clock which hung over the mantelpiece, he said, as if speaking to himself, but so as to be heard by the waiter, "I have had more trouble with that clock than I ever had with one before." Then, turning to the waiter, he went on, "Send Boots' here with the steps, that I may take it down, and I will try once more to put it right.' The unsuspecting waiter told "Boots," who brought the steps. The man mounted, removed the clock, came down, and said to the waiter, "Tell Mr. W. I am busy, and that he must not expect to see his clock back very soon." It is perhaps needless to say that it never came back.

MAC'S POINT OF VlEW—Sportsman, trying a grey- hound : "That dog won't do at all, Mac. It never smelled the hare." Mac "Well, I don't know. It's a good dog—a ferry good dog—shust ass good a dog ass you'll maype get; but the hare wass in an aawful hurry !" In Bavaria the mayor of a little village was ordered by the higher authorities to make out a list of the dogs kept by the inhabitants. He did so, and the list read as follows: "The school-teacher—a dog; the pastor—a dog; the doctor—a dog; myself—a dog; all of us together— four dogs." "1 say, Jim," inquired a young urchin of his companion who was but a few years older than himself, "what does PM. mean after them figures on that there railway bill ? " Jim responded, conscious of his own wisdom. "Penny a mile, to be sure ! " "Well, and 2' " "Oh, that means—that means," said Jim, hesitatingly—" that means a 'a'penny a mile!" •

_ Matttro to the editort THE OLEOMARGARINE 'HILL. SIT,—The pubic must certainly be ir,debted to the members 'who have introduced the Oleoaiar.garine Bill in Parliament. It sounds so much like having the public interest at heart. No seldsbness need be attributed to the butter merchants for doing so (in their owrt interest) two of whom support the bill. The law as it stands is plenty strong enough for any purpose. But the present bill is worse than Coercion, and sounds rather like telling the public they do not know what is good for them. The amount of butterine imported last year was over three million sterling,. This SUM butter merchants view with a jealous eye. The effects of this bill will be to nearly double the price of butter.—' remain, J. T.

ANOTHER JUBILEE PROPOSAL. • Sir,—Will you kindly allow me a little of space in your valuable paper for the purpose of calling attention to, a Jubilee scheme. It is net too late yet, and my Jubilee scheme, if well attended to, and with a very little bit of trouble—for we can't do without trouble even in Jubilee schemes--will last until next Jubilee year. Why can't the shop assistants of Warrington have a half holiday once a week, as well as the shop assistants of other towns? I am sure we (I am an amistaiat) deserve one, and the Jubilee of her most gracious Majesty' emits; be better commemorated than by giving the tradestnerr and assistants a bait holidav every week. Witt some gentleman or gentlemen who has or have irfluence in Warrington (say ikilliam Diggle) kindly, and for the benefit-of -his or their _fellow citizens, take this matter in hand? Summer is _coining on—yes. you may laegh, bet it is coming, but it is like the old-fashioned trains," rather late." The shop assistants, want to enjoy it atEl mach as they can; and if they have a half holiday they will be able to enjoy it more- than usual. The summer nights, at the longest, get 'dark soon after nine o'clock, and the earliest-closing ahem) close at seven, Whlch"leaves only two hours to ourselves. But it we closed on eitlier Thurs- day or Tuesday afternoon the week would not seem so dreary atilt. is now, for could not we look forward to one half day in the week which we might call our own? Thanking von for past favour!, and hoping for a continu- ance of the---oh. I beg your pardon, I thought I was writing put a circular—but it could be done.—l remain, youre . respectful] y,,,

ASSISTANT. THE *WEE LiNl4llitit LIBRARY QUESTION. Sir,f—The,inhablhnits ofcWarringtois are attech indebted to ydu for your' Mine-air lbr this mtion., I beg lon will not cease In youL, good aevork until the goal is won. Why we; In Watrington should have our Pohlic Library maintained tut of rates supplied largely by a plerely mark- ing-class population is more than I can understand. And why "borrowers residing outside the ladrough" should be the privileiged parties they are, because' tbeezcfn afford a penny per, week„jf eaoub h! liewlLiet,,b4g4er intellects than seem to have the management of the Warrington Pub= lic Library. According to the report published by you last Saturday the martens settled. The committee having considered the suggestions offered by the deputation of the Jubilee Committee, and fancying they find in such sugges- tion no primrose way out of their troubles, immediately fall back floundering into the old stagnant pool from which an effort was being made to rescue them. If Mr. Beamont is "opposed to the principle" of a Free Lending Library it is a pity, and only shows how a man may live in the world, and yet farm no part of the world. But, sir, with all due respect.to that gentleman, I hope it is not expected that vte, who are only too really alive to the fact of the world's swift movements, shall not be expected to carry his opinions and-prejudices round our necks like so many millstones weighing us down. Workingmen, demand that the Library shalt be made a Free Lending Library, and as sure as ever straw was found to make bricks of, so shall it be in this case. In other tovins; the words "Free Library" carry with them their true significance. ' In Warringtos, they mean a store room of novels,ic., provided by the masses for the use of ' the classes. Let as struggle on with the questiea until it is ended. In the history ef free libraries, Lancashire has always taken the lead in the movement. We can look with pride to the munificence of the leading men in the cotintv, ex- cepting Warrington. The gift of Mr. Harris, of Preston, of £105,000, and the splendid Brown Library in Liverpo)l stand out clear, and give the county a distinguished position in the kingdom. Bet Warrington ! bless us all, the town is in the most fearful throes to raise the SUM of. £5OO as a testimony of her loyalty. There is scarcely anot'aer object which could be named hhich so powerfully appeals to the benevolence of all sections of society as this of the Free Library. A gift to churches, is a gift te a section, to a party • a gift to a library is a popular gift. The late Pro- fessor 'Jevons says, and truly, "A library of five or ten thousand books opened free to the population of a town may be used a thousand times as much."- It is only those who know the value of quiet study who, can truly say with Pope:—

What an ignoble light it must have been to see the former Tribune of the People, whose locks have become hoary and (body in- firm through a life spent in championing the cause of the people's rights, marching shoulder to shoulder with the very party which he has times out of number stigma- tised as enemies to liberty and progress. How low are the mighty ones fallen I 1 future generation will know, how to draw their own conclusicne upon this last action of Mr. John Bright. It is with rear that I may trespass too much upon your valuable colurrns that I venture to give a few passages from former speeches delivered by John Bright previous to his comitag under the spell Of Lord Hartington and Mr. Chamberlain. hi the House of Commons on the 17th February, 1866, he said "Except en two emergencies Parliament has done nothing for Ireland, and more than that, their complaints have been met—com- plaints of their sufferings have often been met by denial, often by insult, often by contempt" In the following November 2nd, 1866, when speaking in Dublin, he aid—"ls have thought if I could be in all other things the same, but by birth an Irishman there is not a town in this island I would not visit for the purpose of discussing the great Irish question, and of rousing my countrymen to some great and united action. Ido not believe in the necessity cf wide. 0 read and rerpetual misery. Ido not believe that we are ice , ed on this island and on this earth that one man may Areat and wealthy and reveLin every profuse indulgence an a four, six, nine, or ten men shall suffer the abject misery whieh we see so commonly in this world. ,With your soil, your climate, and your active and spirited race I know not what you might do." Twenty years after. April 13th, 1886, speaking upon the first reading of Mr. Gladstone's Home Rule Bill, he said —"I am inclined to believe that whatever there is that is defective in any portion of the Irish people conies not from their race, but from their history and from the conditions to which they have been subjected. . . . I say it would be much more probable that the defect lies in the Govern.

eider as the one before them Would hake sought infor- mation f om towns where cottage hospitals were in existence. He dbought that the meeting should have been supplied with all possible information. He thought a large sum might be raised annually by means of a Hospital Saturday and a Hospital Sunday. lie suggeeted that the question should be adjourned until the meeting had further information. • The Rev. A. M. Wood gave an account of the working of the Wallasey Cottage Hospital, from which be gathered that a similar institution in Runcorn could be maintained for £l5O a year. Mr. Wood pointed out that the ho,pital was not reserved for cases of accident, but that pretty nearly all classes of disease might be treated there. Mr. W. Leathwood, and another workingman named Jones, opposed the recommendation of the committee. Mr John Holt moved the following amendment :—"That in the opinion of this meeting it is desirable that the ques- tion of a cottage hospital be not entertained, as, instead of being a boon to the working-classes, it will tend to demoral- ize the institutions now so beneficial to the working- classes, namely, the friendly societies of the town." M. Holt said the members of the friendly societies ob- je-ted to the Cottage Hospital, not but that' they thought it would be a benefit to a few individuals, but they thought It would be detrimental to the thrift of the working classes. Reference had been made by their worthy vicar to the fact that it was stat: I . othing succeeded in Runcorn. He would point out that en the Jubilee day there would be the celebration of a jubilee of a Friendly Society in Runcorn. Last year another lodge in Huneora celebrated its fiftieth year. Such things as these did not fall through when the working classes took them in hand, and he maintai-ed that nothing that the working-classes of Runcorn took iu hand iell through. They were wodting shoulder to shoulder, every man helping his fellow. They believed that the establish- ment of a hospital in their midst would demoralize their societies, and he therefore moved the amendment. The Chairman pointed out that Mr. Holt' s proposition WRS not an amendment but a direct negative, and therefore those who supported him would have to vote against the resolution of the committee.

r AN Accnniri:Fred erick Dunstan Grimshaw, of Earlestown,was summoned at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, for haying the chimney of his dvlbiling-house on fire, on 25th ult. Defendant said it was an accident, and explained that he placed a newspaper before the fire to blow it up, when it caught fire and flew up the chimney. The Bench imposed a fine of 35 6d, including costs. ALLEGED EY lEZZLEMENT.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Sature- y, before Messrs. B. Houghton, T. .1. , Gillespie, A. C. McCo quodale, C. Pilkington, and W. F. Gooch, Thomas Biro; formerly in the employ of Mr. W. J. Legh, was chargcd b '-r a wa ..nt with detaining certain 1 sums of money, the 1. ..pert vof his employer. On the case being called, Mr. H. Longton, who appeared to prosecute, ' stated that the prisoner's solicitor (Mr. Stuart) had an opportnnity of seeing the hooks and p.pers in the matter, and was satisfied that the e was money owing from his client to Mr. Legh. Arrangements had been contequently made which would result in no evidence being offered against the prisoner, and with the permission of the Bench, the case would be withclrawa. Mr. Stuart would admit that there was money owing from his client, and that the prosecutor was perfectly justified in taking the course he had done.— The Clerk (Mr. Nicholso-.) end he suppolcd they found there was not sufficient criminality about the charge to justify them in proceeding with it.—Mr. Longton said that was so, from what Mr. Stuart had told him.—Mr. Stuart said the prisoner had been employed by Mr. Legh to re- ceive money for sand sold at the sand pit for Mr. Legh. He had to keep certain books, wlich had been kept in an irregular fashion for some time past. He was discharged, and it was then ascertained he had received money for he ehhicad h haecchoaudnnteodt foarcceovnenrytett.ingHbeutthhoe (Mr. Stuart) hadught, however, that found from the books that his client was mistaken in hia opinion. He assured Mr. Pardey there had not bean the slightest criminal intention in the prisoner's mind, and thet it was purely and simply a mistaken idea on his part.—The Bench then stated that they would allow the case to be withdrawn,

"Tax QatvEra " Medal for•Eferoism in the Saving of Life has been awarded to Thomas Whiting, of Stratford-on- Avon who recently caved a woman from drowning at the risk Of his own life. The medal was publicly presented by, the Mayor, Sir Arthur Hodgson. K.C.M.G. Whiting has also received the medal of the Royal Humane Society, in recognition of the same brave cited. Eaaawrows CoNsmosTan CLuz.—The annual meeting of the members was held in the Club, Earle-street Earlestown, on Mondey evening, when Mr M Brown-West- head presided, and he was supported by Captain Seton, Messrs T J Gillespie, T H Pearson, W F Gooch, C F Bor- ron, J Longton, Sze. The Chairman said he had to thank them for the support which had been given to Lord Cross on two occasions, and to Mr T W Legh in returning them to Parliament. The report and balance sheet showed that the club now numbers 180 members, but its financial position is not quite so satisfactory as might have been expected. Mr H J Longton objected to a charge for inhabited house duty, and said he would in conjunction with their secretary, in- quire into the matter, and try to get the charge rescinded for another year if possible. The accounts were adopted. Mr B-own-Westbead was re-elected president for another year, and Mr T J Gillespie, 'LP., and Captain Setoa were re-elected vice-presidents. Mr T Haseldine was re-appointed secretary, and Mr W Melling treasurer. The following were elected ae the Committee of Management :—Meslrs J Catterall, T Bell, J Bateman, A Mawdsley, John Jones, J Greatholder, J Holbrook, J Howe, G Makin, W Sutton S Leather, G Wright, H Houghton, A Mosscrop, and C Lee. Mr J Catterall then moved " That this meeting strongly ap- proves of the coarse her Majesty's Government are taking to protect the person, freedom, and property of the law- abiding inhabitants of Ireland against criminal violence and intimidation." Mr H J Longton seconded the motion, which was carried. A vote of thanks to the chairman ter- minated the proceedings. . •

3PANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. The athonnt of sharer capital, applied for in the Manchester Ship Canal up to Thursday morning reached the total (If 41,940,000. Since Moiidtiy, in spite of the holidays, £llB,OOO has been taledn up. At the weekly meeting, on Thursday- might, of the OldhamCommittee of the Ship Canal Company, the local secretary stated that applications had al- ready been received from the Oldham district amounting to upwards of £190,000 in shares. Mr. Daniel Adamson, in addressing a meeting in I support of the Manchester Ship Canal scheme at Salford, on Thursday night, strongly recommended that Lancashire should raise such an amount of capital as would secure to it superiority of voting power. This would involve increasing the local I capital to £5,000.000. Of this amount it is an- nounced that £3,000,000 has already been applied for. The promoters are increasingly sanguine of 1 the final success of the undertaking.
