LOCAL BOARD. A monthly meeting of the Lymm Local Board was held at the Board's offices at Lymm on Thursday evening. Mr. H. Cameron presided, and there were alto present Messrs Rogers, Thomason, Brazendale, Harrison, Appleton, Dot- ton, Forster, and T. J. Ridgway (law clerk). THE ROADS.—A d'scassion took place on a recommenda- tion of the Roads Committee that Agden-read should be re- paired at a cost of about £3O. Mr. Brazendale contended that the road could be put in repair at a cost of £5, and that it would then be a good road for some years to come. —The Chairman and Mr. Dutton expressed the opinion that the road sadly needed putting in proper repair.—Finally Mr. Rogers proposed, and Mr. Dutton seconded, a resolution to the effect that the road be at once taken up and founda- tions put in, preparatory to macadamising it next year.— An amendment proposed by Mr. Brazendale to the effect that the road be repaired, but be not taken up, was put to the meeting and lost, and the original proposition was therefore carried. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—Dr. Fox, the medical officer of health, read his annual report for 1886. In it he stated that, taken as a whole, the record of the year was the most favourable one that the Board bad ever been made ac- quainted with. The births had numbered 144, giving an annual birth rate of 30 per 1,000, which was below the aver- age of 33 per 1,000. The number of illegitimate deaths was S. During the year the deaths numbered 62, giving a death rate of 12.9 per 1,00. There was nothing to record under the head of" zymotic diseases." The report, which was a lengthy one, referred to the advisability of taking preventa- tive measures against the porsibility of outbreaks of disease. During a conversation that followed, Dr. Fox mentioned that Lymm had the lowest death rate in the Mid-Cheshire com- bined saritary district,which includes the districts of eleven boards. Lymm was the only piece that had been free from zyrnotic diseases during the year. The members of the Board expressed themselves as being highly gratified at the healthy condition of the neighbourhood, and it was decided that the report be printed. , This was the principal business.

BAPTIST CHAPEL, LATCHFOIM.—An interesting entertainment was given in the Sunday school, by the members of the Band of Hope, on Tuesday even- ing. The chair was occupied by Mr. L. Ellison, Who gave a short address, after which recitations were well given by the children, as were also three glees by the choir. Mr. J. Wilkinson's comic temperance song, "Before I had taken the pledge," was well received and encored. A comic dialogue was given by thee females, entitled "Bad luck to the whisky." A dialogue by four males and three females, entitled "Master and men, or how drinking inju-es both," brought the programme to a close. A vote of thanks was passed to the chairman. After the meetirg a petition in favour of Sunday closing was signed by many of those present. , WALTZ Music.—" Cynthia" is the title Of a waltz composed by a local musician, Mr. Frank Booth, and dedicated to the Mayoress, Mrs J. R. Pickmere. The music is tuneful and striking, and will tell well in the ballroom. The principal theme is rather too pronounced in character to aecord with our idea of what is best in music of this class. But in place of the dreaminess and smoothness of this ideal, we have in "Cynthia" a vigour and spright- liness, and a resulting clearness of rhythm, which cannot but commend the waltz to dancers. The harmonising and general treatment of the melodies • are both scholarly and highly effective. An attrac- tive title illustration and clear print leave little to be desired as to the style of publication, the pub- lishers being Messrs. Osborne and Tuckwood. HAREM= HIGHWAY BOA/M.—The first meet- ing of the new Board was held on Thuisday, at Daresbury, Mr. Edward Greenall presiding. On the proposition Of Mr. Long, seconded by Mr. Bradford, Mr. Greenall was re-elected chairman of the Board, and, on the motion of the chairman, seconded by Mr. T. Barber, Mr. Cliff was re-elected vice-chair- man. The Finance Committee was re-elected, Mr. Burgess taking the place of Mr. Houghton. A letter was read complaining of the dangerous man- ner in which heaps of soil had been left on the roadway at Stretton, and stating that a trap had been upset in consequence of the horse shying at , the obstruction, and the occupants injured. I The Clerk reported that he had received a letter from the owner of the trap, who put iti a claim for ' damages amounting to .C 37. A committee was ap- pointed to investigate the matter. SILVER-STREEVSUNDAY SCHOOL.-- The anniver- sary services of Silver-street Sunday School were held in Bewsey-road Chapel on Sunday. Two im- pressive sermons were preached by the Rev. F. C. Haime, of Sheffield, to large congregations, th'e chapel being crowded in the evening. The services were made additionajly attractive by an excellent musical selection rendered by the Sunday School Choir, assisted bythe regular Chapel Choir. In the afternoon a Service of Sacred Song entitled, 4‘ A Child of Jesus was given, the chapel being filled to its utmost capacity. The Rev. G. E. Cutting opened the service with prayer, and Mrs. Cutting then gave the connective readings in a most effec- tive manner. he National Anthem was sung at the close. Th,.7 singing during the day was con- ducted by Mr. A. H. Dunn. The collections were in advance of last year; and the services throughout were very successful. WArturNoroN TRADES COUNCIL. The usual monthly meeting of the above society was held on Tuesday evening at the IlorsemarketLstteet Cocoa Rooms, when the following trades were repre- seAted:— Bakers, filesmiths, wireweayers, wire- drawers, printers, general union carpenters and joiners, glasscutters, glassmakers, and ironfounders. After routine business, a report was read from the representative. in England, of the Toronto Trades and Labour Council, showing the 'misleading in- ducements held out to mechanics and others to emigrate to Canada. It was said that there was work for the next few years and not men enough to do it, but the labour representative affirms, on the other hand, that there are several men in every calling ready to work when there is only sufficient for one. A resolution was passed that the council expresses its sympathy with the Cradley Heath chain Makers, and each delegate promised to use his influence with the different trades in supporting , them. • STARIt - BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY. The I second appropriation meeting of the Warrington Branch Starr-Bowkett Building Society Was held on Monday evening in Legh-street Primitive Methodist Sunday School. Mr. R. A. Naylor pre- sided, and there was a large attendance. The directors present were Messrs. N. Legge, T. Burton, J. Walker, G. Lea, W. Crampton, J. Griffiths, and D. Sumner.-In he course of a brief address the Chairman said that a great ambunt of experiefice had been ac- quir6cl up and down the country in connection with Starr-Bowkett societies, and he was gratified to find that the movement was progressing. A great number of branches had been established, that in Warrington being the 826th, while there were now many more than that number. Starr-Bowkett societies offered great inducementsto the working pepulation of the country and encouraged habits of thrift, and whatever encouraged working. people •to save a bit of money did good and promoted the welfare of the State. (Applause.) •He strongly advised those who were able, to join the society, and in conclusion read the following lines • I now drink good healtlito the eight twenty-slw, - Mid I hope you will see th•i prepriety, • • Of following those who already have joined, This etarr•Bowkett Bulidin4 EkJiely. (Applause.)—An address explanatory of the advan- tages of the Starr-Bowkett system was next given I by Mr. Collins, of Bolton, after which the ballot for the appropriation 7;'as proceeded with. While this was taking place, the chair, in accordance with the rules was filled by a member of the society, Mr. Holford. The result of the ballot was that Mr. Thos. Burton, 76, Liverpool-road, the holder of three shares, was declared to be the successful member. Mr. Burton, therefore, became entitled to an appropria- tion of 000 free of interest for 121. years.—A vote of thanks was then passed, on the motion of Mr. Collins, seconded by Mr. J. Walker, to the Chair- man, and in responding Mr. Naylor said he would be glad to take up a number of shares in the society himself, and as he had no children of his own he would see if he could find' some one else's children for whom he could take up shares. (Applause.)— The meeting then concluded.—We understand that Messrs Titchett and Sons, the secretaries of the society, have received a complimentary letter from Mr. Naylor, who has also taken up twenty-one shares in the society and paid .Cl 5 to clear himself on the books up to date.

• PRESCOT. SAD DEATH.—Patrick Kennedy, of Derby-street, Prescot, a workman in the employ of Mr. John Goldswortb, whilst engaged at Knowsley Hall, on Wednesday in last week, was seized with a fit, and had to be taken home in 'a cab belong- ing to Lord Derby, but died en Thursday morning, He was attended by Dr. Brindle, of Prescot, who said death was due to apoplexy and gave his certificate accordingly. SAD ACCIDENT AT THE CARR'S COLLIERY.—On Wednes- day a sad accident occurred at the above colliery to Thomas and Edward Hughes, of Huyton Quarry, through the fall- ing of rubbish from the roof. Thomas was killed, and Edward was very badly crushed. Ihe latter was attended by Dr. Brindle, of Prescot. On Tuesday the father of the above-named men was also hurt by other stuff falling,which blocked the passage. NEW RATES FOR Itemenur..—Mr H Makin, assistant overseer for Rainhill, applied to the Bench at the Prescot Petty Sessions on Tuesday for sanction to lay a poor rate of 2s 4d in the £, which was estimated to produce £1,578 7s hi. The arrears anionated to £9 9.3 101 arising out of a bankruptcy case. but it was recoverable. The Bench signed the rate —Mr Makin also applied for sanction to a lighting rate of 34 in the £, estimated to produce £B4 16e 10d. The application was granted. Panisn CHURCH SUNDAY SCHOOLS.—On Tuesday even- ing, a service of song. entitled " Eva " (taken from "Uccle Tolll'3 Cabin"), was rendered by a choir of upwards ef 40 voices in the Houghton-street Schoolroom, Prescot. There was a moderate attendance. The chairnsain was the Rev H Mitchell, the reader the Rev D H Stubbs, and the conductor Mr James Heaps. The proceeds will be devoted to the pur- chasing of a harmonium for the use of the Boys' Sunday School, Houghton-street. ACCIDENT.—About eight o'clock on Saturday night, Wil- liam Walker, a collier, of Prescot, who was in one of the swinging boats planted in the Old Park, wanted to get out while the boat was in motion, but missed the rope and over- balanced himself, falling upon John Leadbetter, of Victoria- place, Prescot, and breaking his leg above the ankle. The injured man is attended by Dr. Green and is ptogressing very favourably. Strange to say Walker walked home seeming to be very little worse for his fall. "A COMPLETE MANIAC."—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, Thomas aficEgan' marine store dealer, Prescot, was charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and trap, and also with assaulting P.S. Bull and P.C. Spedding. On Monday forenoon the prisoner, it wee alleged, was drunk while in charge of a horse and cart in High.street. He resisted arrest and assaulted both officers. —Superintendent Barker described the prisoner as "a corn- plate maniac when in drink."—Prisoner was committed to I prison for a month with hard labour A PUBLICAN FlNED.—Before Messrs. W. L. Evans, F. W. Earle. and Captain Wallis, at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, William Forsbaw, landlord of the Hope and Anchor, High-street, Prescot, was summoned for having six incorrect glasses intended to represent half-pints in his pos- session.—Superintendent Barker stated that he visited the defendant's house on the 27th ult., and on examining the glasses he found six of them intended to represent half- pints, about a table spoonful short in each case.—The defen- dant said he did not know the glasses were wrong.—The Bench imposed a fine of 10s and costs. SODDEN DEATH —On Saturday motning, about a quarter past three o'clock, as the police officer on duty in Kemble- street, Prescot, was passing the house ot James Appleton, he heard some one moaning. The police officer asked what the matter was, and Appleton replicd that he was suffering and ask( 1 the officer to burst open the door. The latter, however, was unable to do no, and asked Appleton to , try and open it himself, which he did. Appleton then asked the officer te give him a drink of water, as he was dying which he did, when Appleton expired in his arms. The inquest was held at the Bath Spring Hotel, on Monday, when a verdict of death from heart dinar) was returned. A PRESCOT WITNESS ON FRAUDULENT WATCEI MARE- i5.—The Select Committee of the House of Commons on the Merchandise Marks Bills sat again on Friday, when Mr. T. P. Hewitt, examined on behalf of the Paescot watch trade, said that the trade in England was now in a very de- pressed condition largely attributable to the frauds by foreigners in the matter of the hall-marking of cases. Where foreign cases were hall-marked it was impossible for the purchaser to discover whether the works were English or not. Foreign cases were sent in bulk to the hall-mark- ing office. No declaration was required, and the only con- dition was that the maker should have a known address in England. If foreign watches were sold for what they were worth he would not object. Generally speaking, foreign springs were put into English watches, and chains of foreign manufacture were also largely put into English watches, but in the best English watches English chains only were used. About 75 per. cent, of the English watches con- tained main springs of foreign manufacture. Repeater watches were invariably of foreign manufacture, and he did not think that English workmen had studied the making of repeaters, er what was termed the higher class of watch movements. HIGHWA.Y BOARD.—The first meeting of the new Board was held on Tuesday forenoon, when there were present- Messrs. W. L. Evans, H. R. D'a Willis, J. Leatherbarrow. Lowe, Newton, Tyrer, H. Cross (clerk), Goldsvrorth (sur- veyor. and W. Goldsworth (assistant surveyor.)—The Chairman, ac.: Mr. Lowe moved the re-appointment of Mr. Evans as chairman of the Board for the ensuing year. —Mr. Newton seconded, and the motion was carried.—On the motion of Mr. Lowe, seconded by Mr. Leatherbarros-, Mr. Newton was appointed vice-chairman. Whiston Footpath : The Surveyor reported that the Whiston field footpath was 1,042 yards long in the township of Whiston, and it would cost £25 to put it in repair, and about £5 per year aftervrards. The other portion of the footpath was in the township of Prescot.—Mr. Lowe asked if the Whiston people would have to pay far it themselves.—After some discussion the Chairman stated that the accounts were kept separate for each townshiP, bet the money came out of the whole of the rates collected.—The Clerk thought it was the bounden duty of the Board to repair the footpath, as it was in existence before 1836.—1 t was decided to defer further consideration until the Local Board had discussed the mat- ter.—A Railteay Bridge: Mr. Leatherbarrow asked if the railway company were doing anything with regard to finish- ing Platt's Bridge. The road there was in a disgraceful condition.—The Surveyor stated that he had arranged to send the steam road roller there, but he had not been able to do so up to the present.—Expenditure : Ihe Surveyor reported that his expenditure for the three weeks ending April 28th was: Bold, £5 5s • Knowsley, £49s 2d; Rain- hill, £l6 Os 4d; Whiston, £3 'Os ; team labour, £lO 14s 3d ; new materials, £l7 4s id; incidentals, £1 Os 4d; total, £67 2s 2d.—This was the principal business.

div.p: MARKETS.
LATEST NEWS.
The nomination for the St. Austell Division of Corn- wall has been fixed for May 11th and the polling for the 18th. _ .

The total number of visitors to the Manchester Exhibition up to Thursday was 54,468 for the three days, the heaviest number, of course, being on the opening day. Now that the tithe rent charge has become again due in Wales, notices are being served on the clergy and tithe owners in various parts of the principality demanding large reductions, and it is feared that a tithe war will be at once

re-opened. At Friday's meeting of Colonial Conference discussion took place as to the proposal to extend the present title of her Majesty, and it was suggested that it should be "Queen of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and of the Colonies and Dependencies thereof." SAVINGS' BANES —A conference on trustees Savings' Banks met at the Treasury, and was attended by Mr W II Smith, Mr Goschen, Sir Rivers Wilson, the registrar of friendly societies, and Mr George Howell, M.P., who first brought the matter before the [louse of Commons. The question of the insecurity of depositors, as shown by the failure of certain banks, and other motions were considered. It is understood that important legislation is likely to fol- low as the result of- the conference. -

HANDSOME RECOGNITION BY THE CZAR. VIENNA. FRIDAY.—It is stated from Petersburg, that in recognition of his able conduct La connection with the arrest and conviction of the Nihilists who recently attemp• ted the Czar's life, the Empress has presented General Grosser with a gift of 100,000 roubles, whilst his Majesty, has awarded to the gallant officer an annual pension of 6,000 roubles. THE COLLIERY EXPLOSION IN BRITISH COLUMBIA.

The fire in the Nanaim—o mine, fiCtoria, was still burning on Thursday at 1 am, Of the 138 miners still entombed 75 are Chinamen. After the explosion in the Naniamo mine the pit caught fire, all attempts at rescue being thus pre- vented. On Thursday afternoon the fire was brought under control, but no further exploration has yet been attempted. Thirteen dead bodies have been recovered, including those of seven Chinamen. All those in the mine, numbering 81 whites and about 50 Chinamen, are believed to have been suffocated. The cause of the explosion is unknown.

LAST NIGHTS PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at 4 o'clock. MISCELLANEORS.—EarI ROSEBERY inquired whether the report in the " Standard "of the Colonial Conference was authentic, and when the official report would be published. —Earl ONsLow replied that the report was inaccurate. When revised, the official report would be laid before Par- liament.—Lord Cams said the Viceroy had received no in- telligence of the defeat of the Ameer in the Kyber Pass.— . .

THE "TIMES" AND THE PARNELLITES. o He gave up the premises known as the Old Custom The adjourned debate On Mr Gladstone's amendment to the -*rtardiv- Mr Dillon and the

the Government proposals regarding "Times" newspaper was resumed.—Captain PRICE op- posed the amendment. He thought, under all the circum- stances, as the coantry would not be satisfied without an inquiry took place, the appointing of a Royal Commission on the subject would extract them from difficulty.—Sir H JAMES was of opinion that the motion of Sir Charles Lewis ought not to have been received with favour by the House, as it was a back-banded motion, and he did not think it could have been brought forward in the interest of the member whose conduct was im- pugned, or to vindicate the honour of the House. It had been said by Sir C Russell that if the present case was taken into a court of law party feeling would influence their verdict, but be insisted that no single instance could be given where anything of the kind had ever occurred. As to the proposal of Mr. Gladstone, he Insisted that there was in fact no authority to support proceeding with an inquiry before a select committee. The proper place for the matter to be fought out was a court of law.—Mr. T. HEALY said it appeared to him that the Rouse thought every imaginable subject was worthy to be referred to a select committee by that House, expect the character of one-eighth of its members. As Irishmen they did not care a brass farthing whether they were to have an in- quiry or not. They had not asked for it, but, if desired, they would not shirk it. lie strongly objected to the suggested trial by a jury, as it was absurd to expect that a calm judgment would prevail. —Colonel SetnenEßsOw opposed Mr. Gladstone's proposal on two grounds, first because it was unnecessary, and secondly because it the Committee was appointed it would not have the effect intended. He was proceeding to reply to certain personal observations made by Mr. Dillon, when the SPEAKER intefered, and pointed out the impropriety of lengthening the debate by making recriminating charges.— Mr. W. H. FOWLER supported Mr. Gladstone's proposal. He insisted that the House was the only judge of its ow a honour, and as that was at stake he thought the committee ought to be appointed. If that was done Mr. Parnell had telegraphed that he was willing the letter said to be his should be referred to that committee.—Mr. Irruzs supported the amendment and Sir R. Fowler spoke to support of the proposal of the Government.—Mr. LABOUCIIERE thought it able that in a case where the honour of the House
remarkable that in a was cone.erned the defence of the action of the Governaten‘ had been left entirely to the lawyers. [LEFT smarm.]
